paragraphs.text: Discourses on the idleness of the working of God's good gifts
By Antony of Tagrit, the [?] Gorgias

On the power of the Trinity, worshipped and not made. We write discourses on the providence of God, which brings about good things. It shows and examines how, without compelling free will, providence holds it back from the beginning and from the fruits of sin. They were composed by Antony, the monk of Tagrit.

We are concerned about the dangers facing our fellows, who are troubled about God's providence, who are deeply scandalized and inquire eagerly. So we have come, by a discourse of demonstration that shines out from the paternal and divine light, to set out [?] the matter, while leaving the lofty depths of unsearchable knowledge to their ancient silence. Let no one charge us with a love of probing, or of contention and quarrels over words. We are still taken up with care for the providence that brings about good things, and we have judged it right to [?] this without contempt and without error, and apart from the reproach of the many. For the tongue loves to heap up mockery on everyone who is praised. And it makes it its business and its labour to draw contempt from every word. If someone takes care to grow rich in the good that comes from contemplation, they call him proud, a lover of honour, eager for empty glory. If, again, he loves to keep the humility of the lowly, to hold an unchanging fear, and so to be established as a learned man in the priestly scriptures, or in the praises that the great and good in philosophy are given there, they call him rash and insolent, quarrelsome and pedantic, or rather impudent and too fond of wisdom. So too, if he applies himself to the beauty of the holy crafts, joins himself to humility and to the purity that comes from vigils, and in short embraces all the vigilance of meekness, such a man they call hypocritical and a lover of display, a greedy and insatiable philosopher. These words, then, are seemly and silly, and stand far apart from goodness and excellence. In the very face of the good they strip away the good that loves labour. Let us despise them and tread them down, since our matter is a meditation on divine things. So much for all this. For I have no eagerness to be pitted against tongues

of every kind [?]. Rather, let us turn the discourse to the point against which its force was directed. We are examining the reason why, although providence and diligence watch over our affairs, grievous deaths run rampant, many murders are boldly committed, frequent changes in this life bring suffering, strange rains are brought on, and pestilences of the air spread through the circuit of the lands, along with quakes and tremors of the earth, and conflagrations and fierce blasts of fire that are born from the ether. These and many other things the discourse must open up and examine one after another.

First, then, let us say this boldly: there is nothing that escapes and slips out of providence. Rather, God, who is good by nature, does his work equally and universally for the righteous and the wicked, the unclean and the pure. He does not give way to permissiveness out of anger at sin and transgression, like someone whose wrath comes upon the wicked. Nor does he withdraw his hand from the good because of their care and their keeping of the holy commandments, as though these were enough for them as the seal of perfection. Rather, like an intelligible sun and the creator of perceptible light, he extends to all beings the beauty of existence with fitting care. If a sinful thought and an evil mind, whether in human beings or in demons, sinks to everything that is shameful and disgraceful, we must know that providence is in no way the cause of this suffering there. It is the mind that loves ruin [?].

Someone may say: "Why, if there is providence, does it allow the wicked to speak such things? It would be right for you to rebuke the hand of the bold, to hinder the ways of the dissolute, to stifle the blast of the deviant, to abolish the cunning words of the arrogant and their destructive counsels that hang in the air [?], and to tear up every harmful root, either while it is sprouting, or to destroy it before it is even born." Let him hear this, and not unjustly: providence watches over existing things in two ways. In one way, it sustains and preserves all things as things that were established and brought into being from the beginning by the word of the Craftsman. In the other, when they perish and fall away from the beauty of existence and harmony, it turns them back

to their native beginning. We can grasp this by analogy from some of the crafts of our fellow men, most clearly from the arts of healing. A physician who attends to a sickness of nature works with care and diligence. First, he sees that the body is not troubled by weakness from illness, and so he approaches its treatment by means of suitable foods [?], so that it is not drawn into the danger of disease by bad kinds of food. We know these cases: those who sit at the rich tables of the powerful [?]. And if some humour has grown and multiplied in the body and has begun to lean towards suffering, he supports and strengthens the body with purges made from roots.

So too the Lord, who is great in help. When he has given being to all things from his own being, he cares for them very salvifically and divinely, as things that exist from the beginning. To the angelic and spiritual life he grants immortality and the knowledge of good victory [?]. To material and bodily beings he grants succession one from another, and change that guards and maintains their nature; and to plants he gives growth and fruits. [?] stability [?] and permanence, and continuance with one another, and freedom from diminishing, and the existence of the other [kinds] [?].

For this reason he also guards free will, which is self-determination, that is, our power to carry out with authority whatever we wish of the things within our power, whether evil or good. He guards it as something that belongs to the beginning, and he attends and sees to it that it does not change or perish. Its perishing and change would be this: if someone wished to think or speak, or to desire or do, and only things that are excellent could be thought and done, while things of the other sort either could not be found at all, or, when found, were struck down, so that he could not even be thought to experience them [?]. For if someone is punished and restrained, and is forcibly and violently made to give up the impulse and desire he has conceived, how can such a person be said to have freedom? This is not freedom, which comes under the bonds of force and oppression; this is a form of servile submission.

Rather, freedom is what is ordered apart from the yoke of necessity and compulsion, and has the power to turn wherever it wishes and wherever it pleases, whether into the rugged ways of virtue or into the forsaken ways of wickedness. Consider the things that receive succession from one another through a constant cycle and are no longer diminished. They say that earth, when it is rarefied, changes into water; water, when it evaporates and expands, is cut into air; and air in turn into fire. Conversely, fire, when it is condensed, changes into air, air into water, and water, when it is compacted and thickened, into earth. So neither diminution nor increase befalls them. This is what the natural philosophers say, and also the blessed Gregory of Nyssa in the discourse on the Hexaemeron that he composed for his brother Basil.

In the same way, the goodness of providence toward us, who are bound [to bodies] and human, and toward the free, incorporeal nature, whether one speaks of the good angels or of the rebel host of demons and destroyers, is this: that we live and continue as beings with self-determination and freedom, and that we think and speak, desire and act. If we were to suffer the loss of this, it is clear that we would also be removed from what properly belongs to our nature. The property and distinguishing mark of incorporeal nature is reason, and its fruit is thought. And it is not the property of thought to understand this thing but not that, or to be pure of knowing that thing, which is good, but not this, which is evil. Rather, it is to think about and understand things that are and things that are not, things that stand and things that are perilous, things true and things false, things harmful and things beneficial, and from there either to reject them or to love them. This is the good of incorporeal nature. And in this respect providence fulfils the benefits of God, preserving what is fitting to that nature. If we were destroyed in this, we would be destroyed [as rational beings], and in short there would be left to us a nature without nature and without reason. We would be like camels with high humps, or like the elephant, a tower of flesh. These are like beasts in the multitude of a single force [?]. And this is lifted up with them by natural motion [?]: they withdraw from things harmful

to their existence, whether it is fodder or chastisement or some other need, and they draw near again to things that help and benefit them. They do this not with choice and thought, but driven and pushed by nature. If, when hungry, an animal does not keep away from fodder as long as the food is pleasant, and when it remembers it is drawn to burning desire, then it is startled [?]. It turns aside from a pit and a ditch and from every deadly plant, not with discernment and judgment but through the good of desire, whether of souls or of sights [?], that came into being together with it. So that we may not be like these and be deprived of the good of our nature, providence orders things justly.

That is why it does not restrain the thoughts of the soul, the murderous and cunning counsels of evildoers, the chastisement [?] of the road of men who are murderers, or those who are wanton with women; though at times, and for certain people, it does. And even then it restrains not the thoughts but the deeds, and only where it is especially beneficial. For we know of a case in which a man was prepared for the abomination of murder, or had come to the uncleanness of the bed, and was prevented by some circumstance. Yet he had thought and reasoned, and his mind had not given up carrying his will into effect; he had consented and clung to what is full of shame, and only the seal of action was cast off. Freedom had served in these things, but there it was blunted short of carrying out the deed. Thus freedom naturally strayed [?] toward what is beneficial, as has been said, either for the sake of the one acting, or for the sake of the one suffering, or for the sake of both together, as he knows who is good with authority.

Now someone may say, following the reasoning of the first position, that freedom could be in authority and yet think and feel only these things, and love and fulfil only what is fitting and salvific, either by its own thinking or because God guards it. To him we reply: How, then, do you say that the freedom of the will can cling only to the things on the right? Is it as though some necessity existed naturally with it that would not allow it to turn to what is disgraceful? Or as though, being wise to evil and knowing the good, it kept far from the one as something to be avoided, but pursued the other with all its

strength as something profitable? If it took the first as its law, then our freedom and power are gone, which is the equal path toward evil things or good things, as we argued before. But if the second, we say that it is indeed possible, while we stand in self-determination, to cling wholly to the beauty of the crafts of holiness and to be completely removed from blemishes and faults. These persuade us of it: the souls of the saints who lived purely, and the ranks and assemblies of the good powers.

As for the claim that freedom could be drawn by its own thinking toward the good alone: if this is from God, it is one of two things. Either he guides and leads it by pure commandments and careful counsels, or he hinders and holds it back from daring or clinging to what is abominable. And if he hinders it, again it is either that he forcibly holds back the first offspring of wickedness, stripping our mind of even thinking of it, or that by certain obstructing hindrances he abolishes its very existence. But someone may require that providence should by every means and by force destroy the birth of evil in us. The Good One never ceases to show that this manner [of care] dwells with us. Rather, through every change and every arrangement he takes care that the root of sin be destroyed in us: in some cases through seers and prophets, in others again through angels who are sent, through counsels, through punishments [?], through the giving of laws, through judgment.

But suppose we say this other thing, that it ought first to have uprooted in us the root of evil. Then again it would do harm to the authority of the will. For it is not possible to be deprived of thinking about evil, since we were created rational. And this is not evil. What is restrained is not thinking, but that which, after judgment, a person thinks and, knowing it to be evil, diligently either meditates on or carries out. If we were enlightened only by good thoughts and not otherwise, then for us [?] the good would be a fruit of nature, captured and saved [?], just as fire has its many leaps upward and water its habitual rush downward. And if someone does not say this, but says that evil ought to be something rejected, and seeks by force what restrains it, again we say it would be one of two things: either by violence and force, or through hindrances

and obstacles. And through obstacles, again, in two ways: either through bitter, chastising rods, or through moderate and gentle smoothings [?], or rather, to speak properly, not mindfulness of visitations [?].

If anyone proposes the violent way, he errs. For our good God does not wish to compel freedom; if he did lay hold of it, he would destroy it. Yet in certain cases he does naturally approach this way: so far as he restrains the hosts of demons from troubling our nature or people of honourable conduct. He rebukes and checks their power, as we know from the Scriptures, so that they may not harm the saints. Zechariah knows this, and the book of that victor [Job], and the swine of Legion. So too, in some cases, he brings a violent death on the unjust among men, giving the victory to what is far more profitable, and in a way that flees and restrains freedom. Yet not in every case; it does not happen, but [?] not [?] the many [?], the book of persuasive counsels made you [?]. "The hand of him who stretched it out against him withered," at that time. Moses spoke of destruction and wrath upon men who were full grown in iniquity, by death. Another destruction was that of the cities of Sodom; and the unsparing flood upon the Egyptians; or the baptism of floods in the days of Noah; and the open mouth of the earth for the wickedness of Dathan and Abiram. These, and death by wounds and fractures, with hidden sins [?], which we see continually, are what the strong compassion of the Father brings about.

These come from force, as the discourse has explained. Even so, the freedom of the will is not abolished. For in certain cases it is held back from the destruction that the strong destroyer would raise up, and not man. For that one stirs up many to anger, counsels and persuades, casts down through unbelief and the error of idols, carries off through desire, throws down through falsehood, removes [people] by many quarrels, and by slaughters by measure [?]. So also weak men, when they are led on by freedom, have passed into every form of iniquity and shamefulness. Neither the strength of the strong one came upon them, nor was the restraint of freedom stopped. They willed, and as far as they were able they sealed the desire of destruction. This is what one says in explaining restraint by force. But concerning restraint through blows and chastising punishments, again

we say the reverse of the demonstration concerning force. There they said that whatever force is used for comes naturally to the good. Yet in many cases it soothes and gives free rein to free thought. Here, when he sends many hindrances, often and on all sides, through chastisement, few are stirred and terrified by them. In some cases, when someone begins to be justified, he lays on him illnesses that are hard to heal. And these often do not have their force from nature, as the wise know: many fall ill and come to pains from fullness or from cold, from want or from toil. Rather, he chastises them beforehand. There are times when a person intends to be defiled, and there are times when the mind is ready for this deed, or is at the very beginning of the place of wickedness. In others, by his care he establishes everything: he permits a person to be crushed by strangling demons; or he rebukes and conceals the coming evil, as through fractures; or he puts to shame a multitude of iniquity and wickedness. This concerns those who did not think of turning at the breath of the Spirit and did not repent of wickedness.

He chastises others too. Sometimes he strips them of wealth, when a person had the material for wickedness and the fullness of wrath and passion, taking away his instrument, like the hands of a robber. Such are those who are stripped: either herds of their thousands perish, or they come to an end in their fields and lands. Again, he lets the mind that slips toward contempt [suffer], when he sees the suffering that comes from pride, as in [?], so that it may not be cast into the stain of heresies and that other destruction may not appear. And again, for a person who is good in his craft, he permits him to be weakened by some other suffering, where neither the confession of the Godhead nor hope would corrupt him. And he casts many down through sharp chastisements, he who is our God and cares for all.

Perhaps someone will say in reply: "If chastisement is going to be so profitable, why does it not run at once upon all the wicked and draw them out of the depths of sickness? And again, why does it not come upon each of them many times, so that they might be shown to be pure of all wickedness?" Let us bring this remedy and dressing to that objection. He is wise who [knows] the things to come and all things,

he who cares for all. Or is it something else? I do not know of anything else to say. So the one whom he foresees will gain profit from the chastising rod, and will give up [?] beauty of mind and wickedness, he benefits through chastisement. But the one who, either from his great desire to do evil or from a burning inclination, becomes more wicked through the various kinds of chastisement, he leaves without correction.

That chastisement does harm to some people is well known. We know this from a story. Two men fell into adultery and were caught [?]. One was chastised with a fever of six months [?], received correction from the blow, and came to the depths of virtue. The other was chastised with a quartan fever and severe pains, with the strokes of judgments, yet his adulterous mind neither ceased nor subsided from fulfilling its unjust desire whenever he found respite from it. And since he was like that fool among servants and received no correction from corrections, he became ready for many blows. Whom, then, do you judge it would have helped more: to be left raving in the dissolution of desire, or to be chastised, when the Good One foreknew that he would by no means desist from wickedness? In the first case he would have been liable to one rod and one sentence of judgment; in the second, he is liable to a double reckoning: there for having been defiled by fornication, here both for having been defiled and for having despised chastisement.

But someone says: "Why, then, was such a man chastised with a hectic fever by the goodness of providence? Why did it not leave him unchastised, so that he might be liable to only one retribution? For see, here, by your own account, providence itself has harmed him." To this the true word says that the Lord does not send the chastising rod of death on all such people. For we see a multitude of devotees of astrology, and likewise murderers and men of evil hands, whom he did not afflict [?] even in their children, and who lived their lives free of every danger. But if he chastises some of them, as one who holds to the purpose of example, it is not without reason or without justice that he does so. For

many reproach and accuse providence when they look at the wickedness and cruelty of the worshipper [?], asking why it does not bring a sentence of judgment upon him and restrain him, so that he may be removed from this wickedness. Or again, the man himself, when he has fulfilled his will and repents, will afterwards think: "Why did no chastisement come upon me and hinder me? If it had wished, it would have been [?] my salvation." From such thoughts providence would otherwise be under blame, and they would abound in thought and talk of this kind. So once or twice he crushes and chastises, and in this way restrains the hand that was raised up, so that through this one case we may learn that it would have been just to strike all the wicked like him. But because they by no means cease from evil even if chastisement comes upon them, he leaves them, so that in the destruction of the one who has a double reckoning many may become heirs [?]. And for this reason he strengthens [?] the vigilant [?] hand that was not being forged [?]. But when it was permitted by providence, and fell through passion, then many, growing dull [?] again, [ask] why the wicked prosper, when they see that those who boast of them either ceased from chastisement or grew worse.

Suppose two men fight hand to hand, gladiators [?] or [?] fighters, and one of them falls into the hands of the judge while the other finds escape. The first is beaten and punished: his foot is put into the stocks with long fetters, his hand is bound with chains, and his neck with an iron collar; but afterwards he is released and lives in his rest [?]. No one, then, speaks rightly who says of the one who did not suffer that if he had been chastised he would have become good. One may rebuke this: was the one who was chastised good? No. Then neither would this one have undergone a change from wickedness through the various kinds of chastisement, if it did not come from free will. For it is possible for him to remain as he is, and even to become more wicked, when [chastisement] becomes a discipline for him, like a quick-witted [?] child among boys who, because of school [?], thought of strangling his friend [?]. Thus the law of providence is cleared of what defiled it.

There is also another way to take up the reasoning of the first position. The Good One, like a great physician, foresees the causes of wickedness. To one there is complete health; to another health did not appear,

but his nature is changeable [?], so that the physician lessens none of the requirements of care. While the patient blames his pain for what it is, he meets with kindness in the physician and is not put to shame. But the other, when the physician is wise and foreknows, not only does he not grow careless because of the sickness that holds him, but he grows more vexed and blames the physician, holding it in mind along with his flesh. From this he turns to error [?], though the physician's healing brings him help. Of this kind are all those who, when the True One chastises them gently, make destruction their reward for the chastisement: they curse and rebel, commit every secret evil, and like pigs kicking against the goads, they pass over into destructive wickedness. Thus the first point of the objection is answered.

It remains to show why he lifts the chastising rod from the portion of the wicked, though he is wise about the outcome, and to what end wickedness leads it. For we see many who are humbled as long as they are under judgment, and who are modest as long as they are distressed, but who grow frivolous once they are freed, and are exalted once they are strengthened. And we see a man outside [?], deep in poverty, who, when he regains health through the management of the healing hand, becomes fat and sleek and is nourished on the wickedness of desire. So it is with these.

What then? Through these cases the word of providence remains firm, so that it is not [?] but stands ready in every case, so that there may be no cause of stumbling within. So when he restrains wickedness through chastisement, he does so for as long as the Lord judges good. But when he knows that the one who is being harmed is coming, through this constancy, to a greater evil, he quickly lifts and withdraws it. In short, this struggle establishes diligence: either the one under discipline would never become wise, or he would be [?] from great faults. And thirdly, if he suffers something, it would purify him. For sometimes, if the hand is withheld while it is chastising, a person turns to another wickedness. Learn it from those who hurry to sorcerers and enchanters, so that they either send a person to a demon, or heal the pain of his limbs, when they have despaired of help from physicians. But for others, those for whom salvation lies in being healed of such sufferings, the strokes lead to other, deadly ends [?],

or to those who are purified by the crown of patience and by victory over sufferings, or to those who are ready to turn to a free departure, and for others to cleansing from the stains and faults they have committed. As for those who slip and slide toward the pit of destruction, he supports them by bringing them out and calling them from their pains, even if they are only slightly joined [?] to this.

But the lover of judgments adds a further inquiry beyond these: How, then, did the Judge not foresee that such a person would stray to a demon or to sickness, so that others might also gain this profit? For not all who are lifted up rejoice. And so many perished, or became portions of those who worship demons. Reason, however, rebukes [the objection] in these matters, [pointing] to the great strength of freedom, which is carried into the very thing it should beware of. For when he who holds the ends of our nature pursues us salvifically and at the right time draws the rod upon us, the mind, tormented and not bearing the weight of the blow with patience, drifts toward the end of wickedness. It does not turn to the one who chastised it and hurry to him, though it is he who heals every pain, and he who breaks and binds you, as the holy words make clear. Nor did it wake up to the refining of healing. Instead, as though healing itself were a heavy destruction, it came to what is highest in dangers: it sought relief at the hands of those who serve demons. It would have been possible from there, if that Exalted One had weighed things firmly, for him to drag back the one who had given himself over to this path, although his feet were very weak. But he permits these things so that freedom may be tested by trial and the testing of faith may be revealed.

So when the man who was gripped by a severe sickness in the head [comes] to that evil healer, the priest of the demon: if it is from the rod from above that he has the affliction of his body, then that destructive power of the demon can in no way free him and cleanse his sickness. For it cannot be that what the Lord has confirmed by reckoning should be shown to be overturned by anyone. Instead, in some cases, the pain doubles on him, either because the Lord permits it, or because the demon himself, as one who loves the destruction and wrath of our nature, [brings it]. [Therefore], when he chastises one who [runs] to the refuge of demons, the Lord allows him to find [relief] from his pain, so that, as though not in them while in them [?], the paths [?] may be confused, and concerning the deep fear of demons

may be strengthened. For a demon never moves its dwelling out of a man unless it has received a command, as it were, by decree from the Lord; nor does an illness depart, if it is of help that it should not depart, even if someone, as by a kind of [?], should gather all the [?] of the sorcerers' demons. Experience [?] itself proves this to us. We see many who have been terrified run to sorcerers and enchanters. These display certain phantoms, or make the likeness of a woman speak faintly from the belly, or have the demon itself speak [?] through the tongue of someone who tends goats [?], yet we do not see the people find any deliverance at all from this scourge. On the contrary, there are times when it rages against them more bitterly, or at least as before, to the extent that falling away from God has given it room against them. That free will and unbelief, and not torment at the hands of demons, are the cause of this ruin can be seen from the following. Here is a man who has been robbed and has lost all he had. Another has a wife worn out by barrenness. He ought to look to the Lord, the sweet Pilot, who turns poverty into plenty, and for this barrenness [to look to Him as well]. But because they are of evil inclination and have minds thick with wickedness, they ask destructive demons to restore what was lost, and ask beings that are cunning in every way, and who are adversaries, for the gift of children. Yet when has a demon, a doer of evil, ever given existence to anything or created anything? It is concerned with destroying, which yields nothing. To establish and set up it has no power at all, even if perhaps it once had the strength for this. But we must return to the matter of inclination. There are many who are sick with the feeble impulses of unbelief and are carried along by sovereign free will, and so they have made the means of healing, and the scourges and chastisements meant to turn them back, into accomplices of evil, and have turned the cause of help, conversely, into loss. It is as if someone were to misuse the instruments of the medical art, or the weapons given him to stand against hostile attack, and become his own destroyer: with the scalpel he would cut off his fingers or his sinews [?], and the cauteries

he would apply not to the slackness of his stomach but to his eyes while they are open [?]. He would thrust the knife into himself, and set himself under the point of the lance and the spear, and use [?] more than is fitting. Or as if someone suffered a fracture or a very bad ulcer and went to a physician to have it bound up, and then, because of the pain of the plasters, brought the destruction of the knife lightly upon his own tender neck. In just this way the good law of Providence, through kinds of discipline like these, restrains and holds many back from carrying their evils to completion. We do not perversely assert that it also holds many back and keeps them from doing wrong through the failure of their undertakings, which both is, and is called, custom, habit and nature. For we see thieves, murderers and adulterers who have each taken up the impulse to commit some wickedness and have been anxious to fulfil the desire of their hearts by every method. The one, after toiling all night at breaking in, was caught by a gleam or a ray of light, or by the alertness of the people of the house; and as he fled, he was kept from setting the seal on his wickedness. The murderer, whether pursuing or lying in ambush, had brandished his sword and sprung forward with [?], when, lifting his eye a little, he caught sight of a horseman coming the other way, or a company travelling along the road. Fear gripped him, he took to headlong flight, and remained outside the accomplishment of his crime. In the same way the companion of shamelessness, too, entered the bedchamber, inflamed by evil love and full of joy that his desire would come to fulfilment. Then what? Someone peered in, or called out, and so his whole scheme came to nothing. In a similar way the liar was kept from bearing false witness, and so was the man who seizes by force and takes over other people's fields, and others like these. But in answer to all this the lover of inquiry may perhaps retort: 'Where then is free will? If a man is ready, he says, and has striven in every way, and shown every kind of zeal for evil in order to attain it, and afterwards, without consenting and not at all willingly, he suffers being kept from it, it is clear that he was prevented by force. How then is he free? So, by your argument, there is no free will in such people.'

What do we say to this? Once or twice the Good One holds a person back and draws him out of evil, and that is all. But if He then sees that the mind loves mischief [?], rushes boldly at the deed and hurries to its own destruction, He lets it go and releases it, so that His goodness may be known and free will may be vindicated. This is why we said above that for the most part He hinders, and when it is fitting He steers by force, either for the sake of the one who acts or for the sake of the one who suffers. For example: a woman of beautiful appearance, a chaste woman whose dwelling is always with purity, was loved by the bold eyes of a wanton young man [?]. He cast his eye on her; his wealth was at the service of the deed; eagerly he hastened toward the sin. What was lacking of all that brings an assault to completion? What means and human schemes did he not have? The thing would have been done, had the Good One not been moved on the virgin's behalf. What then? Is it not fitting that this deed be brought to nothing, by chastisement or by hindrance, even if only for the sake of the one who suffers? 'Yes,' I know you will say, 'and by all means.' But if the young man himself had been pure, and had possessed a settled disposition not to fall, the wise Lord would not have troubled at all to hinder him [?], since He sees the [?] of the mind. Let Joseph serve as an example, and a certain virgin, lovely of face, whom first Diocletian loved, and afterwards Tiridates, kings of the Greeks and of the Armenians. Both of them overcame savage lust: he the lust of corrupting women, and she the powers of destruction. Let these stand for the one who suffers. As for the one who acts, there is also something to relate. There was a man, a contender in his way of life, not to be caught by the flesh, who stood far off from every [?], from the waves of lust and the onrushes of anger. By this man a woman, reared in beauty, was seized with desire. Satan the rebel had persuaded her to make bold to this audacity, and she dared to try to lead the man astray. She went into his chamber, as though she were a buyer, and came near to touch him. By decree from on high she was seized on the spot, as a bitter demon convulsed her. And he, shaken by the wonder, gave thanks to his Deliverer. In this way He who arranges the contests for good athletes preserved him from a fall. For He spared

the abundance of his toil, being the Just One, so that it should not be lost through a single turn. If someone says, 'But we see even a man of manly constancy in his art who, when temptation came near to reach him, was defiled and was not helped,' we have dealt with this above. Because he was perhaps about to fall into pride, a passion more loathsome than all, Providence, like a judge, let him fall into a humbling passion so that he might be humbled. There are also times when both are good, the one who acts and the one who suffers, and He imposes a hindrance on both. And if both are wicked, like two men thirsting for blood, how often He restrains them from doing wickedly, lest they come to blaspheme as though care for them had wholly ceased [?]. But if the evil heart does not desist from accomplishing its purpose, the Lord says to free will, 'Farewell.' And when they attack each other with skill and their bodies are pierced through by sword strokes, then they have invited destruction upon each other. So too a frivolous woman came to an assignation with a youth wanton in the flesh. At first the Lord muzzled them once or twice, but they did not give up the impulse of their passion, so He let them both go, to leap upon each other like mares and to suffer a miserable embrace. So much for all this; the demonstration is sufficient, I think. Earlier a statement was laid down: that the Lord exercises providence, whether in mind, or in preserving the things that exist, or by renewing them with power if they are weakened in any way. From this they say that He established and set free will in us and takes care that it should not perish, and that for this reason, so that evil too may be accomplished along with good, He gives these things free rein. Let us therefore inquire by logical consequence: if sovereign free will is the cause of evils or goods, and God is the cause of free will, is God then the cause of both evil and good alike? Let us heal the one who is sick in this way, and treat the ailing mind within him: God is in no way the cause of evils, for He is good and the fountain of good things alone. But if you confess that He is in any way the cause of evils because He established free will in us, give me an answer as I question you: how is He the cause of the things that free will accomplishes? As one who moves

it to do wrong or to do evil, or to do good and be righteous? Can we say that it cannot act without God, like a carpenter's or a smith's instrument, a saw or an axe or tongs, which without the craftsman's hand cannot move to saw, or hew, or grip? But if free will is like an instrument in God's hands, then it is not free will at all, so long as it waits on Him. For that is not freedom which acquires its motion and activity from another and through another. Rather, it is proper to freedom and sovereignty to do and to accomplish whatever it desires and is pleased with, whether praiseworthy or blameworthy. Again, if the deeds of free will are to be imputed to God because He brought it into being at all, what prevents all the deeds performed by the devil from also being imputed to God as His? The argument would then run the same way: if the devil is from God, and the rebellion and iniquity are his, then God is also the cause of the devil's being rebellious and wicked, which is more wretched than anything, even merely to think. In the same way we can also speak about many of the things that happen among us. For example: a man begot a beloved son, and the son became frivolous, or arrogant and a shedder of blood, or what have you. Suppose someone retorts: 'Since the son is the fruit of the father, and this youth is that son, is his father then the cause of his adultery and his wantonness? Or because he murdered, is his father the cause of the bloodshed? For the son would never have come to shed blood had his father not brought him to birth and into existence.' In that case we could not impute to anyone his own deeds, so long as someone else was the cause of his being. But it by no means follows that if the father is the cause of his being, he is also the cause of the rest, these evils. So too with God: if He is the cause of the creation of free will, it does not follow that He is the cause of its evils or its goods. It would be the mark of a mind utterly wicked if this view were to take hold as a rule [?] among men, holding that the Good One is the cause and source of every evil. But so that this thought,

exceedingly wicked as it is, may be driven out of the minds of those who love God, let us set out this one division. The deeds of free will belong either to free will alone, or to God alone, or to both jointly. If someone decides that they belong to God alone, free will is acquitted of evils if it commits them, and of goods if it does them, and becomes neither honourable nor contemptible. If they belong to free will alone, God is cleared of the charge of being an accomplice in its evils, even though He also helps in its praiseworthy deeds when it performs them. But if they come from both jointly and in combination, God appears to us weak and culpable, or, as someone before us concluded, God has a companion and partner in what He does and in what He accomplishes, which is shameful and utterly to be rejected. Besides these, it would follow either that both, God, I mean, and free will, are guilty, or that both are innocent. But let these views be set aside. For if free will is from God, it does not follow that its contrary activities are from God. It is rather like the power of sight in the eyes: it receives its being from the sun, and the giver grants that it should see; but that it sees in this way or that is not from the giver but belongs to the eye, whether it looks at black things or white, ugly or beautiful. No one who reasons soundly says that because the eye became frivolous the sun made it frivolous, or that because it strayed toward [?] the sun led it astray. The sun is the cause only of its seeing; whether it looks far or near, frivolously or modestly, is its own doing. So it is with the law of divine Providence. That free will is able to act belongs to the cause; but that it acts this way or that, specifically and distinctly, that is, toward wantonness or chastity, falsehood or truth, pride or humility, does not belong to the cause at all. Except that when someone does good, God shows goodwill and help, and when he works evil, aversion and hatred. So God is the cause of free will and of its power, while of the kinds of deeds it is free will that is the cause, and not God.

Therefore, if God is the cause of free will, it does not follow that God is the cause of its deeds. And so the assault of the objection that was raised has been dissolved as something feeble. 'Granted,' says the objector, 'let sovereign power come from free will itself and not from God. But why, when His counsel encompasses all things [?], does He bring into being and establish the wicked, who act perversely through their free will? It would have been right for Him to bring into being only the good, whether angels or men, those whose free will embraced the good, and to give being to them alone. Or does the Good One not know everything, and see their wickedness ahead of time, and the sentences they will inherit? It would have been better for them not to exist than to live in such a way that they will be tormented for long ages.' To this we say: it is out of His infinite goodness that the Lord brings into being and establishes the wicked, even though He knows and foresees their wickedness. For this is perfect goodness: to make not only those who will be good, but also those who are disposed to do wrong. Otherwise, should they not come into being at all and not be enriched with free will, because free will acted wickedly? Should what is great and abundant in free will be abolished because of what is base [?] and alien, so that the Good One would thereby be shown not to be good? For is the being and existence of each thing a good, yes or no? Clearly you will say it is a good, if you reason soundly. In the same way free will too is a good, as we judged when we set out the argument about it above. What, then, was it fitting for the Good One to do, if not to bring both being and free will into existence, even though free will was going to err in some respect? Or should He blot these out because of the slips and errors that come from free will itself? That would be like someone whose eyes are bleary, or whose hearing is dull [?], or whose body trembles, saying: 'It would have been right above all that my eyes [?] be removed, my hearing be wholly destroyed, and this body pass into death and destruction', when it is far better that he should see and hear in whatever way he can, and in fact live and go on living, than

be deprived of everything. So for anyone with an impartial mind, the claim that, because free will slips at all and becomes for man, or for the rebel demons, the cause of sentence on account of its transgression and wickedness, they ought not to have been brought into being, is just like someone foolishly saying this: because a man drowned while swimming in a river or a torrent, or in any body of flowing water, and the waters became the cause of a man's destruction, waters ought not to have come into being. Or that because the sun's rays darken the eyes of certain animals and scorch tender blossoms, the sun itself ought not to remain in being, when in fact the nature of water is good and sustains life, and the sun is precious in the eyes of many and helpful in everything, such as it is. Or what someone might say about [?]: that it is destructive rather than beneficial, or that it stands against nature, because it destroyed one man who used it badly, and so the healing art ought never to have entered the world. So those who argue in this way want their God to be evil, so that He should not do what He knows to be good, because of the evil attached to it, even though He is confessed to be good and is not the cause of that evil. For I say this with an impartial mind: it is fitting that God should establish being together with free will, even if free will is going to do wrong entirely, since He is not the cause of its doing wrong. But you, who love being contentious, why do you persist in such foolishness, saying that it would have been just for them not to be brought into being, because they were going to live in this way, and that what is great in goodness should be abolished because of what comes last in evils? That amounts to saying: because I am going to do evil, God should not be good, and should not show in me the fruit of His love for mankind. And along with the rest of your iniquity and wickedness, you are heaping blasphemy and a ruinous curse upon your own wretched head. But perhaps one who is advanced in the discourse of truth will say: 'If, then, out of [?] primal goodness the Good One brings into being and establishes even those who are going

to act wickedly, what prevents Him, since He employs such abundance of goodness, from showing them the way to escape torment and making them members of the household of blessedness?' To this we say: it is not only out of the abundant outpouring of goodness that He brought the wicked into existence and subsistence, but also so that goodness itself should not be diminished and made evil. The one belongs to the outpouring of excellence; the other to the fullness and perfection of excellence. On the one hand, if, knowing without any obscurity that they would offend, He had refrained from establishing them; on the other, if He had not established them and had not shown them the good things that are the Lord's, both in being and in free will, He would be condemned for a deficiency and incompleteness in His goodness. So that if He set about [?] creating in order that His goodness might be known to those who receive it, it was necessary that He should also make together everything He knows to be good. But if, after He made them and gave them being and power, both to exist and to exist well, those weak among men and wicked among angels afterwards sin against the Lord's will, cast away a pure life, take up concern for the things that ruin life, and so contemptuously and willingly reject excellence, and someone then demands that He make them heirs of it even against their will, that person sins and robs free will. For free will is the authority within us to desire and to choose, evil or good. And if it chooses and wills evils, it is not fitting that anyone should bridle it away from these by compulsion and lead it by force, when it desires impure ways of life and the errors of idols; for through these lies the beginning of sin for earthly beings. The punishment of these, they say, is this: being cut off from the knowledge of God, which they loved even here, for they chose not to know God. And through their deeds and their worship, and the [?] which they loved and cherished, they are counted worthy to inherit that too

beyond. And if someone were to turn free will by force away from the shameful things it desired, both here and beyond, he would wrong free will and thrust it out of what it is. Therefore, if free will, for the sake of the desire for wickedness, despises the torments laid down for it while knowing them, and even prefers the torments for the sake of the small pleasure here, it is right that it should not be wronged. For we see such things happening here too, as among those headstrong [?] young men: when one of them is inflamed, burns and runs wild with wretched lust, he would rather accept a sentence of death, so long as he fulfils the wretched lust that has grown strong in him. We have seen this happen with many. We have received it also from the epic tales: how upon Paris, and Ilion with him, upon the beloved sons of Priam, and upon the mighty hero Achilles, the destruction of death fell because of raging lust. And from our own tradition one recalls how Samson, that great strength of the Israelites, through the folly of lust chose to fall from the Spirit and from authority, from judgeship and from honour, and from the might of his strength, if only he might embrace his pleasure. We say this happened in our own time as well, concerning a certain young man who pressed to enter the king's bedchamber and to take his pleasure with its maidens [?]. When he was caught, he was cut apart limb from limb. Like these, we have also heard and seen of wrathful men who, on account of some bold person, mounted up to heaven and went down to the depths of Sheol, because they could not bear the violence of their anger; they grew insolent and cursed even the king. And why recount many cases, when it is evident that many desire and love destruction and extinction, both the kind that comes here and the complete one beyond, if only their love be fulfilled? This, then, is the choice of free will, which is wronged if it is coerced and held back from what it wants. So that it may not suffer this, it is right that the wicked become heirs of fire. Otherwise, if

recompense were not measured out and fixed for the wicked according to their deeds, a very great part of justice would be lacking. First, let us consider the matter when it is put this way. For example, a man practises every kind of iniquity: he commits fornication, defiles himself, kills, lies in ambush, blasphemes, acts wickedly. Which, then, is just in respect of these things: that he be repaid according to these deeds, or that he share in the delight and rest of the saint? But if, so that goodness may condescend, those who lie in ambush are to inherit the delight of the saints, what is to stop the whole host of angels and the assembly of the righteous from raising a rebellious neck against the Good One, so that, when everything is bowed under the yokes of sin, the Good One may be known all the more sweetly? In this way goodness would become an accomplice of wickedness, which is shameful and greatly to be despised. Next, if we examine the other side, I mean when we see the blood of the righteous poured out unchecked, and the injustices done under the sun, the plunderings and robberies along with the whole round of other harms: if beyond there is no just judge, and fitting vengeance is not carried out, these things are wrongs, and those who suffered them are wronged, since here the law of Providence does not restrain or rebuke the wicked. Moreover, besides all this, the account of Providence falls short if the wicked do not drain the cup of their wickedness beyond; it comes close to one of the following conclusions. If over there the Merciful One extends forgiveness to those who acted wickedly, why should He care to restrain evil here and now? Why again did He send His Only-begotten as Saviour, and bring us out from under the yoke of Beliar, the destroyer of souls? On what grounds did He lay laws upon transgressors, to bend and curb their [?] from wickedness? Or again, on what grounds did He bring fierce blows and severe scourges here upon some wicked men, while leaving other wicked men entirely alone, if over there He deals by forgiveness and not by judgment and punishments? For according to this question, or objection, He ought either to requite all of them

here, or not a single one, and reserve them for the reckoning [?] over there. Or what is the reason that one man, though he filled up the whole measure of his wickedness, escaped without punishment, while another was struck here with countless punishments, if over there both are treated alike? For the one who suffered here is wronged by this providence, when his fellow is made his equal in escaping [?] there. Rather, that this one should be chastened here is what his own free will wills. For many entreat and desire to suffer for their wickedness here and not there. Others desire and ask the opposite: to be left to enjoy themselves here, and over there let Him do as He wills, He who is the Founder of the great city, the Judge of all the ages, the Pilot and Lord of humankind. To Him, together with silence, belong all pure glory and praise. Amen.

Another, the second, likewise by him, on the [same] aim [?]: on the chastisement of God; a demonstration of whether the soul departs from the body without God's command; and on the kinds of death.

Once again, then, as we praise the Providence that is over every being, and rely on it as on a wall well built of adamant, and on its behalf offer a demonstration as best we can [?], we say these things to confirm the sincere hearing of simple people, so that they may escape the many thickets [?] of falsehood and be guided along the paths of truth. Let our diction expound what is necessary. For if one keeps treating at length matters on which others have laboured, the thought becomes [?] and tiresome, and is scorned and cast aside, because the subject brings surfeit. And we are caught in the reputation of loving glory, as though we were encroaching on other people's treasures. Next, let our composition be both clear and polished, so that neither the mind is swept by error into [?] obscurity because of the [?] darkness of the things being expounded, nor the contemplation turns aside to [?] because of the [?] meanness of the words used. For it befits contemplation, when it is fairly [?], to be

wrapped in diction like a bride adorned with colour or with a mantle. Together with this, let us take care, with diligence and love of labour, to strengthen and confirm the argument with citations from the Fathers, so that it may not be thought that we proceed otherwise than according to the foundation laid by those men who received the illumination of truth through the Spirit from above. For every piece of writing or discussion that is bare of, and stripped of, the men we have mentioned is rather an empty fancy [?], and brings no profit at all to those who have understanding. But if it holds to them in some respects and is bare of them in others, it has only half its power to profit and be valued. I have said these things because I have confidence of heart in the care that embraces all things. From it I also draw strength and help, as for its sake I venture to offer these arguments to many.

Every trial and every chastisement that, through the mercies of the just Father, is ordained upon the world comes about, we know, for one of four reasons. It is either for testing, as with good people; or for destruction and extinction; or again for [?], as with iniquities and wrongdoers, and with wrongdoers doubly; or to rebuke present evil, or to forestall evil to come, and in a third way [?] to purify what is past. And if a righteous man is tested, it is to cleanse some small fault, or else chastisement teaches him not to sin. These things will be learned in the later parts of the [?]. But the undeserved scourge is the one aim of this treatise, as the discourse has set out. I mean the scourge sent for testing and proving. These four kinds [?], then, come either from outside or from within. For the good law of Providence, coming down in mercy, first turns against what is outside, and through possessions disciplines their owners. Then, if the discipline bears fruit, it rests the scourge and restrains and holds back the chastisement. If not, it begins on what is within and personal. In the first case it kills livestock, ruins crops, or strips thick-grown orchards bare, and the like. In the second it strikes the body, the soul and the children: the body through illnesses, and souls through folly and being overpowered [?].

and through death and destruction to the fruits of the womb. And if by these means wickedness abates [?], and through the strength of the arm of discipline the sin that had grown inveterate is checked and removed, then, as the uplifted arm is lowered, the life-giving right hand shields the person. But if not, the Lover of mankind comes with other, far more severe [?] means: he yokes him in servitude, leaves him in the hands of enemies, and at last brandishes over him the sickle of destruction. For the hands of enemies and of the hostile are a mighty rod, and we know this from what happens outside. But perhaps someone will burst out: Does God will that a person be put to death by the hand of enemies? If he does not, why then is the abomination of murder dared by so many? And if he does, why does he afflict and torment the murderer, either here or hereafter? To this I give the following answer. In one case, for the chastisement of wickedness, God takes care that this should happen, handing the wicked man over to the destructive hand of the murderer. In another case he does not, strictly speaking, hand over; he only lets go. And so that this may become clear to us, let us examine precisely what handing over and abandonment are. By handing over we mean that which God's all-wise hand administers through its help and assistance, and by which it is arranged that a person should suffer at another's hands, as is due to him. Letting go, which we usually call abandonment, is also another kind of providence. It occurs either when God does not forcibly restrain the free will of one who attempts to do evil, while help to the sufferer is withheld, or when he allows and permits the thing to happen. To make what has been said shine out more and become clearer, take the case of an autocrat who has some city under his authority. He deals with it in two ways. First, through the beneficence of laws, through generalship, and through the help

of his hand, if it is attacked by a foreign faction. Then, if the city does not profit from this, and from the height of its prosperity grows insolent and despises its ruler, he deals with it in another way. And if they are [?]... and it is attacked by a barbarian hand, he lets it be chastised by defeats, withdraws from it the help of his hand, and orders his armies away and removes them from it. In this way the wretched city may learn, through hardship and war, how great a good peace is. With this aim, then, the great King and Lord of all is accustomed to make wise and to care for our city, that is, our soul. For when, despite the abundance of his help, we do not exercise ourselves in virtue, he hands over and lets go, and leaves us abandoned in the hands of enemies. That this is so we may show from the saints. When the prophet said of Jerusalem that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came against it, and that the Lord handed it over into his hands, we understand that he handed the city over in the sense that he himself decreed its destruction, and the wicked Nebuchadnezzar served, like a saw or an axe, for the destruction of the unrighteous city. So another seer prophesies: “I am rousing them, and I am bringing them against them; they will not slumber or sleep, nor will the thongs of their sandals be broken—against you, daughter of my people,” and so on. By such words he gives us to understand that the city was taken through help and assistance from his hand. So much, then, for what handing over is. Letting go, on the other hand, is like what we find in Paul, when he says of wicked men that God gave them up to a futile mind, and God gave them up to dishonorable passions, and for this reason God gave them up to the unclean desires of their hearts. In these passages he has put “gave up” in place of “let go.” For it is not right

to admit that this came about with his help and assistance, as in the first meaning of handing over. Like this is also what Moses, the great one of the Hebrews, said about the slayer who had not lain in wait for his victim: “But God delivered him into his hands; I will appoint you a place to which he may flee.” The third meaning of handing over—for this one alone remains for us to examine—is like that in Job. For God said to the Accuser: “Behold, I hand him over into your hands.” And this meaning is one of permission. For, as we showed above, “handed over” in the sense of one who helps is distinct from “handed over” in the sense of one who let go and did not save or help the slain; and that again is distinct from “let go” in the sense of one who permitted this to happen. Now that these things have been distinguished in this way, let us turn back to the question posed earlier: Does God will it, and so share in the murderer's deed? If he does not, why does he let it happen? And if he does, why does he demand a reckoning from the murderer through a sentence, either here or hereafter? We say that a deed is judged according to the intention behind it. If the one who kills intends this—to fulfill God's pleasure—he is to be praised, and with a very great reward. Witness to this is blessed Samuel, who hewed the wicked Agag limb from limb; and Elijah too, who cut down the prophets of falsehood and destroyed them with his zealous knife. His sacrifice was priestly in every respect, and in it the Lord was greatly pleased. For he struck down priests who were slayers of souls, and hence we believe that he received the reward of his intention and of his slaughter. But if the base will of the killer intends this—to quench the furnace of his anger, and therefore he hurries to destroy with the knife and lawlessly stains his hands with murder—then in this the Lord, the Lover of mankind, by no means wills or consents. Yet he lets it go and permits it, and does not prevent it from happening, either to cut off wickedness together with life, as with sinners, or to crown and exalt virtue, as with the righteous. He is well pleased with the one who is killed, but in no way consents with the one who

kills. And since there are two persons, the one who acts and the one who suffers, the Just One breathes great anger against the one who acted, while in the one who suffers his will is greatly fulfilled. That those who kill do not have in mind to please him who lives forever is shown by the law, which stands in the words, “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill,” and “by the hand of man his blood shall be shed [?],” and likewise by those who shed innocent blood. These were made priestly offerings at the tyrant's hand [?], because they would not offer incense or revere the graven image in opposition to the Lord. And the Lord showed their offering to be acceptable, though the hand of the priest who offered it was full of defilement. Hence the punishments of the persecutors are measured according to their intention. So much, then, for those who shed innocent blood. But what will you say about those who killed murderers, and about those who were known for other kinds of iniquity? Did not these too fulfill God's pleasure? That they fulfilled God's pleasure I too say, and I do not deny it; but not when this was their aim. An example of this: one of the kings of our own day went into battle, and one of his enemies met him, speared him and threw him down with a lance. But as it happened by chance, the lance struck the very spot where he had an abscess, and when this burst, the king found relief from the pain. The enemy had been seized by the impulse to wound and destroy the king; the king, however, experienced what he had wholly been longing for. And though the deed was one and the same, by reason of the impulse of the will the one was shown to be a murderer and the other was healed. Something similar we learned happened not long ago to a certain blind [?] man, for he was dim of sight. A youth playing with a ball made of dead animals' skins in the open spaces of the city struck him hard on the eyes, when by chance and accident the man happened to be walking into the path of the ball's flight. Blood burst from his eyes, and light came back to his pupils. And the youth was revealed as a physician and a bringer of light, though he did not

intend it. Here too, although the act is a single one, the intentions of the two, the one who acted and the one who suffered, are widely divided and apart. For the youth wanted to beat his age-mates by sending the ball beyond the boundary, not to make a fountain of light flow through windows opened and unhindered. The other, as he went along, wished perhaps only to reach where he was going and not to be [?] by the blow. Something like this is also the detestable deed that the murderer dares against the one he kills. For while the deed is one, consider how far removed and distant the will of God is from that of the killer. The killer's aim is this: by slaughtering that man to find some small relief from the vehemence of his anger, as we mentioned above. God's aim, however, is that when that person is removed from life he may reap some benefit. And hence God either hands over, or lets go, or permits this to be accomplished. Nor does the murderer know that he has raised his neck against the Lord Almighty, since he stands condemned by the judgment of his conscience, and for this reason of all these things [?].. Now, then, it will help us to consider in discourse how many and what kinds of ending there are to human life, and whether a person departs this life without the command of him who fastened the soul to the body. And so that our discourse may proceed in order and make progress, let it first turn to the ending of life. The ending of human life, then, comes partly from God's decree, partly from nature, and likewise from free will and from chance. And that which comes by decree is partly without cause and partly with cause; and that which is with cause is partly by way of care and handing over, and partly by way of letting go and abandonment. Without cause, then, we call those endings of life brought about by fierce and merciless angels, who sharply and violently rend and separate

the union of soul and body: like those who, while lying down [?], or crying out, or belching, or [?], are carried off. With cause and by way of care we speak of, for instance, common deaths, by which the Good One destroys many, while the Just One increases and preserves certain individuals. Such are earthquakes and tremors of the earth, and pestilences in the air that destroy whole districts, and torments and floods of fire, which at times come from the ether, at times the deeps belch forth, and sometimes they arise in the clouds. These and their like are brought upon the world with providence by him who holds its reins, as he purifies the house that its inhabitants have defiled. You have examples of these in Scripture, in the antiquity of old records, and perhaps also in what you have seen with your own eyes. Those, again, who receive their end from life by way of letting go are those who are seized and strangled by bitter demons, or unjustly killed at an enemy's hand, or destroyed by beasts that devour the living, or bitten and injured by venomous reptiles, or who perish when they feed on deadly herbs. These and things like them do not happen through the providence and help of him who governs the world, but while he looks on and lets go and allows this to happen, and does not prevent it. It is clear, however, that when he has first [?] withdrawn his help, he takes away the shade of his hand and the shelter of his right hand from lives that then ebb away and are cut short. For had he not taken it away, neither demon nor lion, neither enemy nor serpent, nor the poisons that wound, would have thrust anyone out of life. So much the discourse has set out concerning the endings of life that come as if by decree. That which comes as by nature is also divided into other kinds. Distinctly, these are two: a person dies either through disorder or through feebleness and weakness. Disorder is this: through the increase and excess of one of the elements

that prevails in the body, as when the blood boils and suffocates by its abundance; or when the fiery bile increases, torments the body with heat and so drives out the soul; or when the bitter element boils up and with another kind of harm [?] life. And through other things like these, by reason of which a person departs life. For when this comes upon our whole constitution and all our powers, it brings about the destruction of life. Through feebleness and wearing down, on the other hand, the end comes, as it does for the old. For these, even if they escape disorder, yet because their senses have become dull, their strength has already sunk into weakness and the organs of the body have slackened, enter within the fence of death's teeth gently and at the proper time, like an ear of grain gathered in its season, or a beloved vineyard harvested on its day. This gentle death we, or many, usually call—and it is more fitting that it be called so—natural death, because the person has completed the course of his life, and no other cause intervened [?] to destroy it. These other deaths, however, because they are entangled in certain causes, are complicated and bitter, and not altogether close to nature. The death of the old is properly natural, according to the measure fixed for each living creature: one lives three hundred years, another thirty, another three, or near or far from these. And lest someone should say that the way the old depart is itself also a kind of disorder, because of the increase and excess of phlegm—yet this affliction does not come upon all of them. For we see many who died in silence and quiet, when no sickness or pain came upon them, and phlegm did not, as it usually does, disturb and clog their airways [?] and nostrils. They wasted away and sank [?], like a house that has grown old and falls without shocks or blows. So much, then, for the kinds of death that come as by decree and as by nature. It remains for us to bring to light the other pair as well: those whose dissolution springs from the faculty of free will, and those that come as from

accident and chance. Those whose dissolution follows from free will and self-determination happen in two ways. The first, as in wars, in which many are sent down to Sheol, both of the weak and of the hunters [?], as we believe happened in the wars of Ilion and of Jerusalem and of other kingdoms. For it is freedom of the will that summons, gathers and rouses men to these wars, and delivers them to death. The second, as in taverns and [?]. For here, in one place, young men heated with wine, because they drank to excess and lawlessly, bathed one another in knives. Others hired a girl, and after they were stupefied with wine and their anger was mixed with wine, paid her a wretched wage: slaughter by the knife. Such things free will has done when it runs riot with its own authority. Another, a third kind of death prepared by free will, is the destruction of thieves and robbers, whom, once they are caught breaking into houses, the judge's sword slaughters. Others, attacking merchants with a band of men, found that the merchants fought for their lives, prevailed over the robbers and lodged them all together in Sheol. So much for deaths from free will. Those from accident and chance are also of many varieties, of the first kind. As we have seen happen to some people: a sling is aimed at a bird, or a bow at a target or at a moving animal, and someone meets the path of the stone or the arrow, is wounded or struck down, and meets his end from this. Likewise if someone riding is thrown by the rush of his horse and his life departs with the fall. Or again, when someone walks on an old [?], trips, and is taken from life; or when he is lying in deep sleep and is frightened by some vision, and as he leaps up and rises he slips from the roof, or meets a pit and falls. These, and whatever other kinds there may be that are hidden from us at present, we have investigated and found to be ways by which death befalls.

There are some, however, who have defined this fourfold division as a threefold one: the stroke from above, free movement, and that which is as by nature. That which comes from chance they did not consider worth mentioning at all. They rely on the words of David the harpist, who said of Saul, wicked in his conduct: “Either his day will come and he will die, or the Lord will strike him and he will die, or he will be swallowed up in battle and die.” They do not perceive that the psalmist here was not concerned to speak about the kinds of death or the causes that bring death about, but rather to push away from himself the cause of Saul's destruction. Because of this saying, then, many have come to a godless opinion, so as to say that only by a stroke in wrath does God lead the soul out of the body, and in the other ways not at all. And turning to argue against us, they bind us with our own weapons, saying that when a strong necessity prevails over the body—whether the thrust of a sword, or the violence of a deadly poison, or the weakness and feebleness that rule in old age—a person comes to this end [?] even without the command of him who bound soul and body together. To this we reply that those who mouth such things are guilty of a twisted error. First, from the words of the priestly psalmist, who proclaims: “You take away their breath and they die, and return to their dust.” For if, as they say, a person leaves life without a command, this saying is clearly false: “You take away their breath and they die.” In another place too the holy word says: “The Lord of lords does not take away a soul, but first devises a plan.” Next, from what we see happen every day. For there are many whose bodies were severely wounded by sword blows, and yet they did not die. Others, when a blow hurt them only slightly—whether from a teacher's rod or a judge's—departed this life, because he who received them so willed. Others he led away while they slept, and there are some

taken while they were at play. And why do we see escape from the fence of death's teeth for those upon whom every torment came, while to these, who were quite at ease, destruction is seen to come—unless it was by the command of him who composed them that the dwelling of the former was made firm, while that of the latter was uprooted and loosened? For according to the necessity and violence that come upon bodies, those who were hacked by countless swords ought not to have lived, and those who were at rest and at ease ought not to have been dissolved. Rather, the law of providence, which accomplishes good and helpful things, whenever it is helpful, lays low whom it judges right and removes him from life, whether some active cause has been laid down beforehand or not. And with this the vain and wretched counter-argument that was put forward has gone away. And those who set up a threefold division for us, and said that the ending of life comes either by a stroke from above [?], or through free will, or from nature—what will they say when they read of deaths that come from chance? For behold, those killed by an axe that flew off, as we read in Moses: the axe had no impulse from nature, nor from free will. For he says, “He was not his enemy yesterday or the day before.” But neither was it as by a stroke from above [?], for the Lord did not strike him. It remains, therefore, that the fourth kind be confirmed: that the departure from life happens as by abandonment and chance. There met and happened together what the man needed for the maintenance [?] of his life and the destruction that came by the axe. For him who suffered, by the word of him who holds all things his soul was cut off from him and the thread of his life was snapped. That this opinion, which says a person's departure from life happens apart from God's law, slides into deep error—what need is there even to say it? For then the matter would be one of chance and not of providence, as we have said elsewhere. Now, then, it is helpful that, keeping to due measure, which is of great profit to lovers of profit, we bring the course of our discourse to rest here, while to him who lives forever, the Pilot of our lives and Lord of all, together with silence from speech we offer the first-fruits

of thanksgiving along with the gift of all praise. To him to whom it is due belongs glory set free from silence. Third Discourse: On the question of the term of human life, and what its end is. By the same author. We approach the third contest, standing with the Word, him who has the word of our life. We do not dare to pry, but we show, as far as we are able, what the matter is. We trust that we shall not be put to shame, since we do not walk outside the right aim. And let our discourse here too be complete and not deficient, measured and not overflowing. For if it is poured out and spreads beyond measure, it bewilders the mind, burdens the thought, and brings contempt on what is set out. Rather, just as for ships there is the harbor, for laborers rest [?], and for travelers the inn, so for a mind that has toiled and meditated in contemplation there is quiet and silence from speech. So much for this. Let the discourse now turn back and return to its aim, as we examine whether our human life is indeed bound by some defined and measured term, and whether it is fixed and decreed how long a person shall remain in life according to the good law of providence—that is, of him who has authority over our life. For many ask, inquiring and investigating, whether one who departs this life—whether by strangling, by slaughter, or by sickness—had of necessity to be removed from life here, at this time and in this way, and could not have lived any longer. The answer to this we shall give by drawing on the thoughts of the Fathers, which we arrange at the end of our treatise like a seal, a crown and a guard—for the purse, the head, the house and the city—so that it may not be plundered or despised, nor be led astray by fables. For now, let us give an answer from our own reasoning, first making this declaration: human life is defined and known, and the time when it is extinguished [?] and taken away is fixed. That it happens in this way or that—I mean through various and diverse causes—is not already fixed; but that life is fixed and defined by a certain appointment we demonstrate from the following. What do you say, sir? Is

the entrance into the world of each of us fixed and known to God—when it is to be and in what manner: that Noah would belong to such a generation, Abraham to another, and Moses likewise—yes or no?
