But if it is not fixed and known, then the matter is one of chance and not of providence, and the joining of soul with body did not come about with reason and through the Word, but, according to the fables of the many, who say that it is a matter of nature: when the womb, being fertile, receives the seed that is cast into it, then the soul is brought there and created by God. This is for the most part not credible. For that one woman is more fertile than another, more able to bear fruit and to carry a child, is admitted. Yet the Good One has many times restrained fertility, and in the same way has overcome infertility. Scripture too demonstrates this in what it tells us, when it speaks of the wombs of barren women. Likewise nature itself teaches us that fruitfulness comes about irrespective of when the seed is cast. And the Good One, as and when it is fitting, binds the soul to the body, whether there is fertility or not. This we know happened also with the world. For the Sower of the world, though he was eternally contemplating its creation, established it together with time, and will dissolve it together with time and reason and [?], in a definite way: he who holds its reins appointed a beginning and an end for the world. Therefore Gregory, the chief of the learned, says: “You who make all things, and transform and change them by your craftsman Word, at the time and when you know it to be fitting, in the depth of your wisdom and providence.” In this same way, then, we must consider our human life as well. For the time of our entrance into the world is fixed and defined by God, and likewise the time of our departure is measured and defined. But perhaps one of the glib talkers will burst out against me, saying: If a man had not left his house at that hour and gone on his journey on business, he would have escaped the murderer's blow; and if he had not ventured to cross the river

when he rashly went against the force of the current, he would not have drowned. So the cord of his life could have been stretched further, and it is not defined by any appointment. To this wretched reasoning let us give the following rebuttal, first with Scripture refuting it. What answer do you give me on this, sir? Job's sons and daughters—if they had not been under the roof of their elder brother's house, then even if they had not perished through the collapse of the house, would they not have perished some other way, just as fire consumed the shepherds, as the story tells? In this way we must also reflect on the deaths of many. For just as there destruction carried off together the young people, lovers of companionship and pleasure, and the flocks in the fields and folds, so too the end of death overtakes us when we complete the term of life and our departure from life [?] arrives. Next, we have a story of something that happened a little before our own time. A certain young man, near the city of the Assyrians, was crossing the Tigris river by a bridge built of boats. Coming toward him, a soldier driving his horse struck the youth with its rush and plunged him into the river. The young man's wretched fall was seen by the crowd of men standing by the river, and they ran and secured the saving of his life. Not long afterwards, when he had gone to his lodging and was celebrating his rescue with the many who had saved him, and feasting pleasantly, evening fell. He went off to vomit, dazed both with wine and with sleep, slipped on the roof, struck the ground, and came to rest in the bosom of Sheol. Experience too demonstrates these things. For we know of many who went into battle, took countless sword wounds, and were pierced by the thrusts of spears and the shooting of flying arrows, and who, when they turned back and returned from the war, faltered [?] and were not delivered from the circle of death's teeth. And there are others into whose very souls the sword went, and whom people already counted among the slain; and when the physicians who search the field, those who accompany the army,

came and found them still breathing, they carried them off and restored them to health. This same thing happened also to one of those merchants who are lovers of profit. He was traveling toward the East with a large company when robbers overtook them, and they fought hand to hand. When those wicked men had sent the crowd of his companions to Sheol, they also struck this man hard with a sword on his tender neck, and he was counted among the slain. A day later, when some villagers were searching through the slain, they found him gasping, picked him up and carried him away from there, and by the labor of physicians they greatly strengthened his weakened life. And he lived fifty years after that. “Yes,” says the opponent, “look—you have strengthened our argument. For since here, when other souls were being drawn away, it was granted to him [?] to live in the same way, what else happened but that the measured term of life can be prolonged? A sign of this is Hezekiah, who, though he had received the sentence, ‘You will die and not live,’ afterwards had fifteen years added to him.” But I, my good man, say this, and I do not judge wrongly: if the term of this man's life had not been set and fixed at a later time, he would have been crushed, together with all the rest of his companions, in the jaws of the destroyer [?]. But because the thread of his life was yet to be extended further, it was not cut at that time. And though the cause was pressing hard, the Good One made it void, procuring for him help from life. But if you say otherwise and decide that there is no measure to our life, and like a good athlete meet your opponent with his own weapons, then answer me when I ask a small question: Does God's knowledge know the things that are better and the things that are to come—yes or no? If it knows them, and knows them definitely, and knows, wills and brings about the better things, then it must also bring about the dissolution of human life in a definite way.

when what is better is seen together with the departure. There are four points: knowledge, efficacy, the term of life, and the benefit in the cutting short of life. As for efficacy joined with knowledge, we do not recognize it in God in every case, but only where it brings benefit. How so? He knows, as the source of wisdom, all the shameful deeds that people have committed or are committing, yet he in no way aids or assists them. But he acts when he knows what is better, as is said in the Gospel: "My Father is working until now, and I too am working"—that is, in the governance and preservation of what exists. Of what kind? That the sun should rise; that the grasses should spring up again and the animals bring forth living young; and that, in the first place, immortality should be attained within mortality, through the succession that springs up by birth. Since we said that the Good does not also bring about everything he knows, let us, for the sake of consistency, bring this to mind as well, even if we stray a little from our aim. We say that he does not bring about even everything he is able to do, nor everything he wills. For he wills that we should not turn aside from the holy commandments, that our hands should not be stained with murder, and that our bodies should not take on the shamefulness of fornication. Yet although he wills these things, his efficacy is in no way brought to bear so as to make us abstain from them by compulsion. Let us know too that he is able by his power to make innumerable worlds, and that he could create for a human being wings for flying and feathered [?] wings, eyes in his feet and a horn on his breast. But he does not do so merely because he knows and is able. But let my discourse hasten back to its aim. If God knows determinately our departure from here and the length of our stay, and when he knows, he brings it about because it is better that it be so, then human lives are indeed determined and measured. And if this is true, let those change their tune who say that human lives are something loose, now drawn tight and now stretched out, like a piece of wood drifting to and fro on the waters; that they wander and float about without knowledge and without determination, and are like a ship without a rudder, with no beginning or end. But perhaps, it will be said, God is not bound by a term,

and if he wills he lengthens life, and if he wills he shortens it; for who is he that stands under the yoke of necessity? And do you bring a term to bear on God—or rather, do you take "term" to mean fitness and good order? But if you think the former, you go very far astray and spring away from the truth. For God, who set order in the things that exist, is not a God of disorder and confusion. If, however, by "term" you mean some compulsion and tyranny in which God is entangled when he determines lives, this we reject, and our mind and our speech pass it by. For we believe in God and confess that he knows necessary things in the mode of the possible, determined things not determinately, and things subject to limit not in a limited way. He has no necessity as we do, so as to be confined within modes of the possible and the necessary, nor does he, like our knowledge, perceive knowable things either in a general way or distinctly. How so? We know determinately the things that come about by nature—for instance, that the sun is luminous, the earth dark, the wind in motion, the soul alive. This, which is given by nature, we know distinctly; this is what learned men call necessity. But the things that are not bound under nature we know in a general way—for instance, whether or not we will be rained on tomorrow, or whether or not we will share or love. These they call contingent. In the same way, things that are confined, and confined by spatial limit, we grasp with a mind that conceives spatial limit; our materiality cannot conceive of a limited body with a thought of limitlessness. But God, the wonderful, holds all these things, as I have said, above us rather than as we do, in power and in wisdom. Therefore he is not himself confined under necessity and term; and though his own strength is exalted above these things, he has subjected us and our lives to term and to the necessity of beginning and end, so that we might not be despised and scorned, nor become estranged from order and be cast off [?]—he who from the beginning has bound up and governed the creatures. For it would be shameful if he who

set a term to night and day, and with time measured out for all living creatures their birth and growth, their dwelling and their corruption—so that even the stork and the swallow know the time of their coming, as the word of Scripture says—should leave us to fall away and stray from these. But if you say, on God's behalf, that it grieves him to have his authority diminished, and you tell me that it is written, "If he wills he lengthens life, and if he wills he shortens it," I too accept it, and I send up a sigh mingled with lament over those who are troubled in this way. I likewise say that if he wills he shortens life—adding, though: if it helps that he shorten it. And I say that if he wills he lengthens life, knowing, and not overlooking, where the completion of life lies and when it helps that it should not turn aside. And again I say that if he wills he lengthens life, and he is able and has the authority to accomplish this; but he does not will it when something else is fitting and more beneficial for a person. For the saying "if he wills he lengthens, and if he wills he shortens" establishes for us that God's authority is indissoluble and his power capable of all things. So the formula is taken in a sound sense: if he wills he does this, and if he wills, that. Yet when it comes to what is fitting, it rests on the manner of his governance. Hence it was fitting for the king of the Israelites, Hezekiah—since he was not mistaken about the end of his life—that God should decree the lengthening of his life through Isaiah's message. "You will die and not live," he prophesied to him. If then the completion and term of the king's life had been fixed there, and it would not have helped him to live again, but rather that he should then and there be brought forward to his departure, the prophet's announcement would no longer have called for the pouring out of tears from that point on, together with the instructions concerning his departure [?]. For Hezekiah knew that he had been [?] by the weakening of the illness, and that the force of the sickness was dissolving his body, so that he should hasten to give his household his parting words. But with such a word he who is the source of all help acted for his benefit, so that he should not suffer from the sickness of pride, as one through whose excellence the power of the destroying angel had cast down the hosts [?] of the Assyrians. Therefore, when the spring and the hope

of renewed life, as it is called, returned to him, he cried out and proclaimed with praise: "I said that in the height of my days I would depart." The height of days, say those who are trusted in such interpretations, is the abundant prosperity that he had established through righteous prayer, by which he laid low the legions of the Assyrians. But if someone reads, according to the [?] text, "I said that in the midst of my days I would depart," even so the sense fits the view we have set forth. For this is the midst of days: when they have been stretched to thirty or a hundred, and afterwards are cut short and drawn in from their extension, like a thread from a rope that is snapped and frayed. How then do these things make it clear and plain to us that human lives are held within a certain term and measure, which in common usage we call an appointed time or set term? We do not presume to say, like those afflicted with the malady of dotage, that there is some decree and fixed sentence and term laid upon God, because of which he is in no way able to lengthen or prolong earthly lives. For who has laid this necessity upon him, that among the first inhabitants of the world so-and-so and so-and-so should live, and for others he should cut life short, and stretch them only as far as a hundred or eighty years, like fixed terms? Rather, fleeing from this, we draw near to what is the beauty of piety. And that we may flee error, we say that the Good has given us the term of life as the laws of his providence, while he governs what is of great help to us in the course of this fleeting and wretched life. He acts as an immeasurable height, whose wisdom made the worlds, and who brings us out into life and leads us in from life, at the time and when he knows that it helps; and he does not leave it to nature to come about of itself and steer wherever it wills, as with a horse running headlong, or to the course and rush of the wind that never stands still—which, of all things, is without understanding and beyond reason even to contemplate. Rather, when the points set forth above fall into agreement with the truth and settle with us, they also bring the word of that Compassionate One, uttered through the prophets,

into our midst—that word in which God, making a promise, said: "If I speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot and to pull down, to overthrow and to destroy, and that nation turns from its evil, I too will turn back from what I had purposed against them." And on the basis of this word, they say, God is not subjected to the compulsion of necessity. But to those who mutter these things let us gladly say this: we are not putting God under the yoke of necessity, my friend; these things are not under necessity. For we are not so utterly devoid of perception and understanding as to make him who is above all power and authority bow beneath compulsion and submit to necessity. It is not decreed upon him that he should measure lives in this way like a prescribed number, so that the course of his work is sealed from morning to evening. Rather, as the treasury of all discernment, he has measured and appraised lives by foreknowledge, seeing what is fitting for the servant at the right time: how long it helps us to dwell in the life of the flesh, and when it is expedient for us to be cut off from it. And if we do not accept as true that God is Lord of both, binding and loosing, and that he distinctly knows and keeps the time of each, we are compelled by every constraint to confess that our affairs happen at random and by error, and proceed and are administered without God. But lest I set a stumbling stone before the word of that Lover of humankind, I will make this clear to you, so that you are not harmed and suffer great loss through an unprofitable hearing, as though the word of God were [?]. For that treasury of help is helpful in using the form of a threat so as to turn people back, and in putting on the countenance of one who is angry, since his eagerness is for what is helpful. Hence too, through Jonah the seer, he prophesied to the Ninevites the overthrow of their city, while giving room for their repentance and their deliverance from evils—not because he did not know whether they would repent or not, and thus whether salvation or destruction would befall them; but this was being arranged by that power which is above all arrangement, so that, hearing the threat, they would melt away from their evils and repent, and so not suffer what was threatened.

Had he not desired this, it would have been very easy for him to destroy them suddenly, and he would have had no need of the swallowing of the fleeing prophet. Destruction did come upon them a little later. For in the fullness of time they withdrew from the fruits of their works of humility [?] and turned back to their wickedness. And in the days of Nahum they received the judgment they deserved, without any prophet being sent. For since they had learned it once for all, they despised the forbearance of the Spirit and the kindness of God, and no other preaching was needed to admonish them. Rather, with stupidity and foolishness they kept saying, "Where are the words of the son of Amittai?" For just as a cloud had covered his words, so they mocked the words of any other preacher as well; and so they became workers of their own complete destruction. Formerly, then, he had sent and, through Jonah, guided and threatened them, neither mistaken about nor concealing the term set at the beginning and the end that would come upon them without fail; and in the days of Nahum he took them away. But it was so that the many, those in whom there was a leaven of virtue, might through the word of threat and rebuke turn and be brought back from the labors of wickedness, and salvation from judgment might dwell with them. Just so a wise man of great understanding, the guide and teacher of many children, corrects the dull and senseless by force of his hands and the strap, and carries out his training of them silently and without words; but the others he reproves with a word of rebuke and gently bends them toward virtue, which, more precious than pearls, is learned by a free mind—though if even the blow of a word brings them no benefit, he judges them in their ill fortune as he does the dull. In the same way God too, the guide of all, strikes with the rod of discipline those who are dull and wicked and who do not melt at a word; but those who through admonition receive [?] conversion he wins over through messengers and envoys. Therefore he destroyed the Sodomites, great sinners, severely, in silence and by judgment, for he knew that they would never be made whole by words. For how could a messenger have helped those who, even toward the angels sent for their destruction, as those who would fill up the wickedness of their fortune,

he set them up [?]? But the first inhabitants of Nineveh he guided through the word of an envoy, and turned many of them back from the toil of evil; and in the end they received the judgment of the Sodomites, when they took up again their former deeds. And from contrary elements, not at a single time, they received a doubled sentence of judgment: for the river that ran through the midst of their city and the fire that burst out from the works of the desert—the one purged the earthly part, while the other consumed the airy part. These accounts teach us this, as does the word of Nahum, which cries out in figures about their judgment. But perhaps someone will say that God lies, in that he promised such-and-such or such-and-such, and did not carry out the oath he had sworn to his servants. To this we reply with an everyday example. If a tutor says to a boy, "I will thrash you and beat you," and pours bitter, sharp words into his ears, intending—and this is his aim—that through threat and fear the rebellious part in him may be rooted out, and that he may have no need of compulsion by hand and blows, do we then say that the tutor lied, because he promised the boy that he would beat him and did not? Not at all, if we look to his aim and intention, which is that in this way the boy might be kept within proper bounds [?]. It would have been fitting to add a condition to his statement: "I will beat you if you are lazy in your reading." But since, in promising "I will beat you," it suffices that the boy understand that it is a word for his own benefit [?], the word of a tutor that is joined to a threat, it was not necessary to state it with a condition; it is applied in the understanding. In the same manner, then, is the word that the Compassionate One used toward the Assyrian race: "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown"—that is, if they do not repent. And since this aim belongs to the statement, we say that he did not lie. For if he had said, "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall by all means be overthrown," and afterwards, when this [repentance] had taken place, it had found escape from overthrow, then perhaps he would rightly be charged with falsehood. But he said nothing with a condition, nor that it would by all means perish; rather, it was shown with a view to the fulfillment of his governance that, in order that they might repent, the word of threat was devised and made a declaration [?]

as to why, and until when, this city Nineveh would be covered [?]. With the same understanding, then, the word was delivered through blessed Jeremiah. For when the Lord made him hear with a condition attached, he said: "If he speaks a word, not of evil or of good, concerning so-and-so or so-and-so, and they turn and forsake their evil or good deeds, they will not suffer what was purposed"—not as though he truly and without condition held fixed the time of their destruction and the end of their ruin. For it is determined and distinct for him that as long as they show contempt, multiply [sins] and grow corrupt in the face of the threat, he will then destroy them. But if they hold to it—and he foreknows this—then he does not bring it to completion upon them at that time; and likewise this is in his foreknowledge. How well the Assyrian example that was adduced has refuted [the objection]! Why then, they ask, did Moses, that guide of the Law—or rather he who speaks through Moses—command that parapets be built around roofs and a covering be placed over a cistern? Was it not so that he might keep himself clear of a deadly and harmful death? As he himself said, "lest someone fall and you say, 'This happened to me from the Lord.'" Well and good; I do not contend against this. For I know that the Lover of humankind and Just One is in no way a stumbling block to anyone, and that he takes care not to be thought so, and lest many incur judgment through an unjust thought. For this reason, since the cause of destruction was free choice—in climbing to the height of the roof, a person, distracted and befuddled with sleep, might be pushed and fall, and then make it a pretext against God—he warns by his word that parapets be made for roofs. As those who make the demonstrations in the treatise preceding this one show, the kind of cause that brings about the destruction of life is distinct from the end and from death. For the one has God as its cause, not in every case, as we have refuted; but of dissolution and departure God is the author in every case and through every cause, as we are showing. As for that Mosaic saying, I have heard others interpret it in this way, and it too helps to support the firmness of our position. For they say that the Hebrews had learned from their dealings with the Egyptians about fortune and fate: that fortune is something like

what happens by chance and error, whether in evil or in good; whereas fate is something decreed and determined by the governance of the heavenly powers, whether they err or do not err, and there is no escape from it. So, then, lest through this teaching they should grow sullen and blaspheme in misfortune, or think that there is no providence, as the notion of fortune holds, or attribute to God the cause of evil and good, of misery or affliction [?], and not to the act of their own freedom as is fitting—so that they might not suffer these things, he gave them a useful command and removed them from erroneous thoughts. So much for all this. Let us now turn from here and come to the vain idea that is in the air among us [?]. Look, they say, we see a weak man who rashly charged a troop of cavalry, and they put an end to him on the spot; had he not done this, perhaps he would not have died. To this, my friend, I reply: Have you not seen or heard of a mighty and confident man who grew bold against weak men, and met his end from a single one who threw a missile? I, at any rate, have heard—and not without reason believed—that one who often prospered in wars and battles was brought down by a weak man. Indeed, the Good rebukes the arm of the lawless powerful man, the mighty man who relies on his own strength. Let the divine child persuade you, who with a sling killed Goliath miserably. There are also men who, though the strength of both was equal in arms and they fought one another together, cut each other down. And sometimes a weak man kills a mighty one, and a mighty man in turn kills one strong of arm, or a mighty man his fellow. If, as the foolish think who said it, the weak man's rashness against the troop brought about his death, it would follow that the mighty man killed by the weak one must confess that his dissolution came from no other impulse than the word of him who binds. But if the Lord of power has given the mighty into the hands of the weak, it is plain too that he delivers the weak into the hands of the mighty. In the one case he sweeps away the strength of sin; in the other he establishes and corrects lives conducted in sin, while in both he looks to what helps. As for what was foolishly said—that had so-and-so not done this, he would not have been brought to dissolution—it amounts to silly mockery. For this argument could be run through every matter. If a person did not eat too much, he would not fall ill; if he did not become overheated, or chilled, or were not seized by some other harm, he would not suffer the compulsion of sickness.

This foolish reasoning is refuted as follows. If a person did not eat, he would not have movement either; but since he eats, he must be moved. And the sinner would not be put to death by the bitter blow had wickedness not been sweet to him. And the head of our race in the beginning would not have been estranged from the tree of life and from paradise had he not tasted of the tree of knowledge. But since wickedness was sweet to the sinner, and to Adam the fruit and the [?] of separation was sweet, the one was handed over to destruction at the end, and the other to wretched exile. Therefore, since God foreknew that, although it was possible for the sinner not to be harmed by sin, he nevertheless willed and carried this out—for had he not sinned, he would not have been swallowed by death—because it pleased him to sin, God also determined and appointed the dissolution as one who helps. For the Good does not know contingent things in a general way, as our freedom does. We indeed reason this way in our wisdom: had a person not gone into battle and war, he would not have been overtaken by the end; and had another not gone into the house whose walls were tottering, he would not have perished in the house that collapsed. But God knows and foresees that, although it is possible for this man not to go into battle, he is the more eager to go into it, and that he has no escape from slaughter, and that he looks [?] to it. It is not that this satisfies him by [mere] ability, since he does not know it in a passing way; [he knows] the departure and the seal of the action—not as we do, by guesswork, that if not so-and-so, then not so-and-so. For if, because a man entered beneath the shelter of tottering and leaning walls and was killed, it had to be so, the same outcome ought to have befallen the others too. Yet we see, and also hear, that in the very same house, where many were lying, one, they say, was snatched even from the jaws of death, while another met his end at once. But he said that he had been hidden under a vine [?] or a beam or something else, and found escape as if by chance. And many, from mere fear at the collapse of the house, were seized with derangement, and the terror at the excavation of those buried joined them, shattered, to astonishment and amazement—they who without suffering or blow saw the end of men crushed out of life. Others, however, that

Good One saved; and when they were violently thrown down from the height of a roof, they did not die. Another, feeling a small jolt, went at once to Sheol. To others, out of deep abysses and violent, rolling surges, that Good One granted deliverance from drowning. An example of this is Paul's ship, which rested on the back of the outpoured waters and was broken into many pieces, yet we do not hear that a single one of its sailors was carried off by death. But of others we are told that when their ship was broken up by the waves, it cast away its men together with its cargo, and all went to the prison of the jaws of death. So it was with Odysseus: when his [ship] was shattered, the storm-wave saved the man of many counsels and drowned his companions of evil deeds [?]. Of these matters we have also spoken above, and so the account suffices as it stands. How then, they ask, do these agree: the end at which the life of the one who died was completed, and the will of the murderer or of the one who administered the deadly drug? It is a marvel, they say. Nor am I myself left out of the astonishment of mind that moves me to offer thanks to the Lord, when I marvel greatly at the greatness of his governance. Yet I say that since it was helpful and greatly salutary for the life of the one put to death, and it was fitting that his dissolution take place here and in this way, [the murderer] was moved toward the dissolution by the Lord's governance; and the hidden hand ran, seeing the visible hand, and delivered the man from life. But if it had not helped for him to exchange life here, it would have restrained the destroying hand, as we often discover. Likewise, had it not been fitting that he die in this way, it would have chosen for him another kind of help, whether strengthening or merciful. But if he who holds the dispensations of the world in his hand foreknew that a cause—poison, fire, a crash or a collapse—would reach this person, and he let go the care of attentiveness, and did not effect the word of deliverance in life, but [allowed] his dissolution from life as was fitting, then it necessarily follows that he be added to the judgment and that it increase, and that he be crowned at the judgment [?]. So much for these things. Now, however, it is needful—as we bring to mind the question of what the end is, and remove it from error and from fate—that our treatise proceed [?], illuminated by the testimonies of the Fathers.

We find, then, that "end" is an equivocal term, and in many passages the word of the saints reveals its meaning according to the context. In some places it is taken for limit; in another for a blow and the rod of discipline; sometimes for a cause; in places for demonstration and knowledge; and elsewhere for payment and wages. Where Scripture, praising with care the work of God, says, "He set an end to darkness, and to the uttermost bound he knows," it takes it for limit. For he who is the author of evening and darkness makes the day by the change of the sun; when the sun's disk runs beneath the shadow of the earth, then God establishes the order of night, darkness. Therefore the victorious one says, "He set an end to darkness"—he who is order and limits. Again, when he speaks about providence in Job [?], saying, "He leads the wise astray and destroys the words of the pure, and brings an end upon the righteous and the sinners alike," and afterwards adds, "all these are from the end of his ways," he takes "end" for cause, so that the sense is this: from the cause of his ways—or rather, his judgments are incomprehensible—those who are governed in this way. Moses used it for demonstration when, as though from the person of the Lord, he said, "The end of all flesh has come before me." For "end" here is taken for the showing forth of the decree of their judgment. This is clear because "end" fits none of the remaining significations so as to be taken there. The seer Habakkuk took it for the blow and rod of discipline: "The end will come and will not lie; and if it delays, do not lose heart [?]." For payment and wages, Ezekiel and the beautiful Gospel use it: the one said that he did not lend at a settled rate; the other, that he settled with his laborers for a denarius a day. For here "settled" and "settled rate" are taken for payment. Indeed, one might also take the word "end" for the term of life, in what David examined when he said, "To every limit I have seen an end, and your commandment is exceedingly broad." These meanings, then, we distinguish, so that we may escape [?] the snare of error. Let us understand, when we call death by the name of "end," in which of the significations mentioned it is taken:

[?] in the sense of that which decrees judgment, or that which is with term. For these two we do indeed use when we interpret the departure from life. So much concerning the end. Fate, however, is a vain [?] thing, from which it is [impossible?] to [?]; it is opposed to and destructive of freedom. Likewise, it is in every respect foreign to chance. Chance, in turn, is a certain impulse apart from the will of the soul, arising from rational or irrational, animate or inanimate things, which proceeds and comes about indeterminately. It too is a deceiver and a harmer of the governance of the household. When, therefore, we say that human lives are determined, and decreed and fixed by God, and that the end overtakes and comes upon a man from God, we wish to turn wholly away from these erroneous and godless notions. From that of chance we turn, when we confess that order and measure are decreed in the beginning and end of lives by him who gives the soul together with the body, and at the proper time releases it from life, and again binds it in the fullness of time, and inseparably. From fate we flee when we do not in every case blame and attribute to God the causes of life and of those separated from life. For it is not fate that one man dies miserably in this way while another departs blessedly, but he who renders to deeds as in the balance of the scales—even if he removes some from life either by handing them over or by permission, while he does not bend them beneath compulsion, and does not choose to step in to bend our freedom. Therefore he often uses permission, and handing over rarely and on occasion; for handing over is close to necessity, while permission is joined to freedom, since it permits and leaves it free to turn as it wishes and as far as it wills. Concerning fate and chance, let these remarks suffice for the present. What is lacking in this account you will have from us in what follows, if God permits, so that the labor may be ours in love. Now, however, let the testimonies [?] of the Fathers come in, so that we may not be judged to be saying strange things when, with term, to human lives

We read: from Basil, from the discourse entitled "That God Is Not the Cause of Evils": Wealth is taken away from those who misuse it, so that the instrument they use for iniquity may be destroyed. Sickness is brought upon those whom it profits, so that they may be chastened in their limbs, or so that the powers in them that incline toward sin may be held back. Deaths come when the limits of life are fulfilled, limits which from the beginning received God's just decree concerning each one of us, since from afar He foresaw what is profitable for each of us. And a little further on: It would be very fitting to consider that when people suffer from deadly and incurable illnesses, these are aids that come from His care. But when the suffering proves greater than any relief, it becomes necessary to cut away what has been corrupted, so that the sickness, creeping on little by little, may not spread to the vital parts. From the Theologian, from the oration on his brother Caesarius: "O Steward of our souls and Doer of good things, who made all things and changes them, setting them in order by Your craftsman Word, in due time and as You know, in the depth of Your wisdom and governance: receive now Caesarius, the firstfruits of our departure. And if the last goes first, we yield to Your words, on which all things hang. Receive us also at the last, at the fitting time, when You have guided us for as long as is profitable." The Theologian did not name the "limit of life" openly, as the blessed Basil did. But by putting "in due time and as You know," and "receive us at the fitting time," and "for as long as is profitable," he gives us to understand that there is a limit to what is profitable, and that for as long as it helps we live, and in a certain measure, and that at the fitting time comes the disclosure and the departure [?]. From the holy Ephrem, from the discourse against Bardaisan: God foreknew that those slain by murderers would have their life limited by that slaying. Yet He is far from the wicked one, so that it was the murderer who dared and killed; and far also from chance, so that the slain was not slain by accident. If, then, the slain man

did not go at his appointed end, it is chance; and if he went at his end, it is a stumbling-block. But God is above both chance and stumbling-block. It was not chance, since his end had drawn near; and it was not a stumbling-block, since judgment is to come. Yet although these things are well resolved, they still need resolving, for it is hard to see how there met in one moment the hidden end of the slain man and the will of the murderer, so that the slain should go at his end and the murderer be guilty at the judgment. That the body should be separated from the soul is God's creation; but that the soul should be separated from the body, that too is something granted for its benefit. And if anyone thinks it credible and needs it for the truth, there is the book called "of Steps," which is passed around in many mouths with contention and division as to whose it is: some say it is Evagrius's, another says it is Eusebius of Caesarea's, others that of Macarius the Great among the solitaries, and others that it is the work of Philoxenus of Mabbug. To it we refer him; and when he comes to the seventh discourse, which is written on the commandment of the upright, let him learn from there. That it is not foreign to [?] Then there is David's "Behold, You have given my days by measure," and our Saviour's "Are not two sparrows sold for two pennies?" and the like. Since these are read and known to everyone with little effort, we pass over them. These are the proof-texts of the Fathers. As for the rest, let it be prayer. For I pray and bend the knees of my heart to the learned, that, fleeing from fault-finding and love of strife, they may cleave to the plain truth, and that this work may not be despised by them because of the weakness of its author. Let them flee from envy and heed the saying of the blessed Ephrem, which persuades most aptly and counsels thus: "When," he says, "the strong and the weak follow the scent of water, even if the weak happen to find the spring, the strong enjoy it with them and rejoice together; they do not, because the weak found it, hang back and scorn it, and out of great thirst murmur from envy." So too those who seek the truth: if it happens to come into the hands of the weak, let it not be rejected while we are sick with the sting of envy. To God, who greatly helps me. And upon me

may He in His goodness cause a glimmer of understanding to shine, and in every way rescue and deliver me from evil, and in every undertaking and every word strengthen me as its partner, its finisher and its honourer [?]. And by His clear glory and through His exalted knowledge, here and there may He show that it has pleased the One who is fitting [?]. Glory to Him who sets free from silence. His fourth discourse: on the law of providence, on chance and fate, and also on poverty and riches. By Antony of Tagrit, who is reckoned a Gorgias [?]. Sweet is the fruit of toil. And, as sound judgment loudly proclaims [?], it is the source of all good things. One finds that the slothful man is made a mockery at every turn [?] because of his laziness; onlookers count him worthy of every contempt and feel no pity for him when they see his misery. But the diligent man, who has toiled much and laboured and grown weary, and whose fruit and enjoyment have been doubled, they honour and magnify, and along with his good fortune they give him praise as well. And if it does not come into his hands, and he loses out and is left without fruit, they bring no blame upon him. Therefore for me too, since care and diligence are laid upon me, and a sign of the immortal is set about me [?], to examine providence with a little of the knowledge of God, to show how great it is and of what kind, and to proclaim it free of fault and reproach, it is fitting that I look with the eyes of the mind to the treasury of the diligent and the industrious, and become like those who dig channels and wells, who dive into the depths, and who delve in the mines after silver. For all these together, as many as dig in the depths, with all this toil gain fruits: flowing, abundant springs gush forth for them, and many cold streams; the diligent miners find ingots of silver from small veins; and from the depths divers, heedless of their lives, draw up precious stones. And without [?] I am reminded through the servants of the love of toil and the fruits that come of diligence, I say; and through the weakness laid upon me I am held back from the discourse that was held to be appointed for our speech. Yet looking to its Father, I approach the discourse with prayer, so that it may proceed for us in due order, and that the words which push providence aside and draw many to the mire of evils [?] may be overturned; and so that, as for dark paths,

we may shed light on them through the word of truth, and make people turn away from them and become lovers of God. These things are, as we agreed in the discourse before this one, which was treated at length, concerning the names of chance and fate; and I add besides concerning accident, injury and mischance, and any others like them. Fate is a necessity from which there is no escape. It divides into two branches: some say it comes from the stars, while others refer it to God. It took its beginning from the teaching of the children of the pagans. For they handed over the governance and providence of the things on earth and of this whole universe to fate and to the revolution of the [?], saying that through the conjunction of the seven wandering lights with one of the twelve signs of the zodiac, abundance and suffering, happiness and glory, birth and death, poverty and wealth, sickness and health, understanding and contempt, and a host of other occurrences are portended. And as for the voluntary conduct that belongs to free will, I mean modesty and chastity, mercy and cruelty, these too, as one who apportions them, are allotted to happen, and there is no way, they say, to escape or evade them. For example: when Zeus stands in a certain position, a man enters the world as a king; when the sun is in Aries, a strong and valiant man is born; and whoever is in Aries together with Leo, they say, will be a thief and a murderer. If Kronos is in conjunction with Scorpio, a bitter and cruel man is born at that hour. From Hermes they seek eloquence, and from Aphrodite beauty, wantonness and good fortune. Thus they assign the providence of this universe to the revolution of the wandering and the fixed stars, and to these they entrust it. This is the first meaning of fate, from which this foul stench comes; and these new pagans who said there is fate caught its scent, agreed in everything with the old pagans, and wronged the works of free will. Harms and amendments, honours and torments, they ascribed to necessity. They differed only in this: they confessed that these things are determined and allotted by God, and that everything, they say, is written beforehand on each person's head: what sort of person

he will be and how he will fare: whether an unbeliever or a wanton, a believer or an adulterer, shameless or full of modesty, a slave or a labourer [?], freeborn or [?]; in short, wretched or blessed. And this, they say, is from necessity. Chance, on the other hand, branches out into many doors, and is in every respect the opposite of fate. For they say it comes either from fortune, or from mischance, or from injury, or from accident. Fortune, for example: if someone falls while drawing from a well, or finds a treasure, or is struck blind, they judge this turn of events to be apart from reason and diligence and assign it to good or bad fortune. Again they say: so-and-so took a beautiful wife, rivalling the sun and moon in brightness, and was filled with shrewdness and understanding; and this man they call fortunate. Another, while he was on the road, had all that he possessed taken by a band of robbers, and they left him half-dead; and they pity him and say, "Alas, so-and-so is unlucky." Accident they apply to falling from a roof, or a sprain, and other blemishes that afflict the body. And mischance is like when someone passing through the market is struck and wounded by a drunken or mad man with a sword or a club; such a thing they call a cursed mischance and an evil encounter. Injury, too, comes out in the same way as those already mentioned. Chance has a borrowed name, like a river in flood that sweeps away and carries along with it thick trees and oxen from the herds, and whatever it meets. For example: so-and-so the governor was angry; and as he took vengeance and punished the offenders, he gave orders [?], stirred up his men [?] and had them flogged, saying, "Do not spare!" And when they began the punishment along with the offenders, those who had not transgressed also became the work of the sword: by chance they slaughtered good and bad, cut down meek and fierce, friends and enemies alike; and so-and-so perished by chance. The head of this door was Epicurus the philosopher. For he held that the world has no maker, that it is eternal and unending, perpetual and ageless; and moreover that it has neither guide nor helper, but came into being of itself, moves along without a pilot, and receives renewal, as the serpent grows young again

and casts off its old skin through long fasting and through narrow crevices [?], and as the eagle in flight renews its limbs and grows young again in life through the drying of the sun's rays and through a spring of flowing water. In the same way he said that through floods and fires and deadly vapours the world is purified and acquires renewal. In the same way he said of human nature that people have been and are and do not cease, being renewed through the succession of birth, and that when one dies nature finds another in his place. In the same way he dared and was bold enough to speak of the races of animals, of the roots of plants, and of the cycle of the elements into one another. Many have inherited this disease. They have filled the whole expanse of creation. And they have filled it out of fear of being reckoned among the despised door of fate; and they did not discern which is the royal road and path. For it is fitting, since our minds are beset by these evil heresies, that our thought be harmed neither by rashness nor by mischance. Indeed this counsel presents itself to us, namely the shrewd and aged thought: that we keep far from fate and also from chance. Let us not, out of fear of fate, say that things happened by accident: that when two are blinded and suck the venom of the serpent, one sits up and finds escape, while the other is bitten and the mass of his entrails is cut through in the pit of his belly [?]. Nor let us say the other: that it was allotted and determined that the man who committed adultery and murder could not have been chaste and quiet, that it was sealed and decreed. For both of these opinions are senseless: the one which decrees that all things are without reason, and the other which says that all things alike are by reason and design, and which robs us of the roots of free will. Rather, while we assign the things of governance to Him who stands as Lord over the world, we must believe that He wounds and heals; that to one He extends the term of life, while for another He cuts it short differently, knowing that a longer life would be more harmful. But the things of free will let us leave to the one who does them. For it is not the case

that they are allotted by God and that there is no way to escape them. For if the works of free will are counted to God, and we become like an instrument of His will, so that He accomplishes either evil or good [?], then first we would come to [?] our conduct like a beast without reason. And whatever passion stirs the powers within us, we would not refrain from carrying it out. After that, we would come to spurn and despise laws. For why should laws be needed by those with whom necessity is allotted, and which does not allow them to live by laws, since their nature has come by chance to [stand in] need of laws [?]. Third, all disciplines would cease, and people would no longer feel the need for strict diligence in any art or science. Scribe and elder would not submit to correction and teaching under discipline, and the smith and the carpenter would not make peg and [?], door and chair. For what use are effort and discipline, if, whether a man is taught or not, he is going to be a skilled and expert scribe of every kind? Or why should the carpenter or the smith toil and weary himself, if, whether he toils or idles, he is going to have vessels of every kind? And with the abolition of laws, discipline and craftsmanship are destroyed. Even justice would cease: good men would not be crowned, nor would transgressors be punished. Just as the serpent cannot be praised for fasting long, nor the eagle for its wing growing great, nor the peacock's wings be praised for the weight of their feathers, nor the peacock for its beauty, nor the lion for its strength, nor the elephant for its size (for each of them received its glory from nature and did not will to be what it is, since it did not exist before it willed), so too the humble man would not be praised and crowned for his fasting and his vigour, for the beauty of his soul and his endurance; and likewise the dissolute would not be blamed, nor the base disgraced, just as we do not humble or disgrace the dog and the fish for greed and voracity. Along with these, accountability and [?] they push away and reject as if from their side; and still more those who think the governance of the great world and human affairs move as if by chance. For

how is it that, like a horse that has slipped from bridle and reins, it runs with mindless force, leaps hither and thither and goes headlong, and wanders recklessly to whatever place the force of nature likes; and like a ship well fitted for the current [?], which is driven by a gust coming at its stern and thrust disgracefully onto rocks [?] and into whirlpools; so it is held by some fortune and wanders aimlessly wherever it pleases in the course of life, whatever happens [?]? Then let a man abandon the work of the mind, cease, and be stripped of its fruits. Let him not think of marrying, nor of sowing, nor of reaping; but let us marry foolishly and in ignorance, and like cattle and wild asses tear our food from the ground with sharp teeth. In short, let all our deeds be done by us without knowledge or understanding. From here the movement of contemplation would be crushed and reckoned a matter of spontaneity. But these things are far from us. For since we were created rational, it would be the height of folly for our deeds to be governed by chance; and since we were made freeborn, to be driven by the compulsion of fate is also despised. Yet as they make chance a fellow-worker and nature a path, they say: "See, we observe that certain causes arise from nature which overstep the limit. Sometimes the rains are abundant and destroy; at other times their abundance is helpful to seeds and plants, and to the land and its inhabitants; so nature brings it about. For example, the winds shut up in the belly of the earth, when they grow and gather strength, cause cities to be shaken by earthquakes, and so many are rolled down into Sheol. In other places, when they gather strength, they come out of their hollows, and at their exit springs of water gush forth. With the force of nature the air too comes and is cooled, and sends many burning fevers [?]; and for many days it destroys through frost, and damages what grows on the earth. In [?] it humbles the strong pride, strips the ears of grain of their fruit and the trees of their blossoms and fruits together, and causes countless other losses. When it becomes very bright, it boils with the strength of the sun in summer;

along with these, the inhabitants of the south are long-lived, while those in the north are wretched and short-lived. In one climate beauty prevails, in another an ill-favoured appearance [?]." These and similar things are said by those who act as advocates for chance and have every argument on behalf of nature. But what do we answer them? Simply this: everything in our nature comes from and is guided by Him who fills the world, both in these domestic things and in the falling away from these domestic things. He brings about sameness and changelessness in the elements, in animals and in every kind of plant, looking to the help that comes to human beings from that sameness; and He brings about the many changes and disturbances in the elements and in other things, looking to what helps more. For this reason certain causes work along with nature, so that when we are entangled in the winds of sin we are harmed by them; but when we walk aright, not only are we not harmed by them, but we are greatly helped. Hence He permits the region beneath Olympus to be shaken by winds, and He slackens the winds of the air, which through showers and dews make the growth of the seeds shine, and do not repel the splendour of the sun's rays [?], so that, being heated and scorched, they bring about great dangers [?]. He loosens the bound of the sea and carries off the inhabitants of the earth. These things He does who spoke to the sun and it did not rise, who brings the winds out of His storehouses, who in the beginning set the sand as a bound for the sea and hung the earth upon nothing, and who can govern all things by the nod of His will. For when our mind is slackened toward the disorder of sin, He lets go the reins of the world, and it too passes into corruption and disorder. And because we did not give thanks for the things by which we were honoured, and do not draw near to what is profitable, we are disciplined by these very things, and learn strength from what we suffer, since we did not come to know from what was good for us, as the Theologian says. Hence He permits the winds that dwell in the hollows of the earth to shake the world and to bring about the overthrow of cities and the destruction of their inhabitants, as the good Ephrem said: "The earth

spoke out against iniquity, for it could not bear to be beneath it." And the great David: "He looks upon the earth and it trembles; He touches the mountains and they smoke." That nature, when it is slackened and released from the reins of governance, is driven forward by a disorderly command, this shows: there is a certain great mountain in which tremors and quaking occur time and again, and surely we know that it is ready for its inhabitants [?], since they are not deserving of destruction [?]. And if this movement and force of wind were not restrained by Him who stands over the world, surely the force of the slackened wind would show itself in its neighbours [?]. Another place, though no great wind had gathered in it, was violently shaken by the force of the wind, and many perished in it; and a few people unexpectedly found deliverance. In this place, by the providence of grace, one man lay covered beneath a roof for eleven days, as if in the bosom of Sheol; and people burying the dead passed by him, while his groaning showed where he lay. So too we hear of the sea: though it is often stormy, and year after year rolls its waves and gathers strong force, it does not overrun or flood the land that borders it, since this law of life holds it in check and restrains it. But at times, when it is released by a nod and finds slackness, it brings great destruction upon cities and upon the islands within it. And the sun, when it scorched, gave drink [?] to a multitude of offspring and afflicted the fruitful power of plants. These and similar causes He who brings [?] all things allots together with the whole of nature, so that through sufferings we are gladdened when we walk aright, and are chastised when we turn aside and sin. In every place and at every time, the measure set apart and given by God for help and delight He turns into punishment wherever sin reigns. And just as composition preserves all bodies and food nourishes them, which took their beginning from the four [elements] in fours, so too mixture and disorder, stability and agitation, each of them either permits, or slackens, or destroys. Hence a land measured out for sowing, in which a harvest of grain grows abundantly, He puts to hire [?] for this through [?] and captivity, and through famine He judges and destroys [?] its inhabitants. And again where

there is some pasture, fat and thick with gardens and woods, He spreads deadly vapours and casts down its inhabitants, and from the air above them He brings their multitude to an end. And there are places where, through a swarm of creeping things and locusts, He lays waste the land unexpectedly and without warning, burdens the air, and cuts off plenty together with life. In short, in every place and at every time, the measure set apart for delight is sent out for torment. But surely someone will say: "We see that after such-and-such a time a plague killed many, while a yearly flood destroyed the inhabitants, and some of them were saved by fleeing to the mountain." It seems to me that whoever says this does not know the power of God at all, of which the great David said in praise: "If I go up to heaven, You are there; and if I go down to Sheol, You are there too. If I lift up my wings like an eagle and dwell at the end of the sea, even there Your hand will take hold of me and Your right hand will guide me." And another prophet, concerning the Israelites who wished to remove themselves from God's yoke and were placing themselves under the shoulder of the Assyrians and the Egyptians, said as in the person of the Lord: "They came to Egypt and went to Assyria; wherever they go I will spread My net over them." And yet another said: "As when a man goes out to the field and a bear meets him, and he goes into the house and leans his hand on the wall and a serpent bites him, so is the day of the Lord: darkness and not light." Such is the power of the Lord when it is exalted over the wicked. For when a town or a city receives a blow, as if weighed out upon its head [?], woe to him [?] who wishes to escape and be saved. "For the earth is the Lord's, and its fullness," says the psalmist in priestly fashion. If not by this, then by that it hunts him down, and he does not escape the net of destruction, unless he is bound by the law of righteousness and takes refuge in the covenants of holiness. So it was with priestly Jerusalem. For when they defiled the conduct of their lives and angered the Holy One of Israel in their sanctuary and their priesthood, through mighty angels

their end came. Only those, they say, escaped judgment who, through the zeal of him who was clothed in linen, received a mark on their foreheads, he who examined them for their observance of the law and their purity. But if someone found deliverance from a place that was being trampled down, having removed himself from that place, like those who escaped the flood by going up the mountain, we say that he was found in this remnant of advantage and leaven of repentance. And so they also say that he escaped judgment when God moved him, or a holy angel urged him, or his conscience changed him, so that he changed his place and found life, and was not cut down by the sickle brandished over the wicked. For the sharpened sword and the drunken sword do not mingle the blood of the righteous with that of the wicked, teaching that one should not love the dwelling of the wicked, which brings about the ruin of many. For this reason the righteous Lot was exiled and brought out of the defiled place through the mission of angels. And from among the wicked Babylonians He calls and draws His people, saying through the prophet: "Flee, flee from Babylon, and do not draw near to it; whoever is found in it shall be pierced by the sword, for the Lord has willed that His will be done in Babylon and in the land of the Chaldeans." This, then, is how the Lord, suffering long over the righteous with mercy and pity, visits them, exiles them and brings them out of a place on which destruction has fallen, and shields and hides them from the angel of death: whether through a holy vision, or a diligent angel, or a prophet and seer, He moves them from there, as we have learned to say. But if someone, by the freedom of his will, flees from a place that has provoked anger and is condemned, either he will surely not find escape, if he does not cease from his wickedness; or, if he does find it, a good thought was in his heart, for whose sake he also shook off and abhorred the place [?]. It is for us, then, to say that he should be strengthened in goodness and bring forth fruits of repentance. For it is not by spontaneity, as if by chance, that people escape death; otherwise this would hold: that some escape death and the destruction of the flood even while living in the very same place,

while others, even after moving away, come to an end and die, either of the same illness or of another kind. We see the like with other chastisements too, for example with locusts or hail. For when the good angels who are set over our protection, benefit or care are sent a judgment to decree against us, so as to turn us back from the mire [?] of wickedness, they carefully direct hail or locusts upon the fruits of their fields; and we see this happen. For a cloud of hailstones, while it is hurrying along somewhere, certainly strikes; and within one boundary and one stretch of land, the field of the wicked man is beaten and crushed by hail, while that of the righteous escapes. And in one region and one district we have heard of two villages lying side by side, of which one suffered complete destruction of its fruits by hail, while the other was not harmed in the least. And what is wonderful: the cloud is guided by an angel like a twisting serpent. Its course runs from the west; it visits one village and passes over another; it rises toward the north, and while it ravages some places there, it turns toward others in the east or the south and grinds them down; and many in between it leaves alone, without loss or harm. Here one may marvel and see the work of nature, how it remains and stands under governance: for the mass of the clouds, when the winds drive them from the west or the east, guides them along a straight path, and with their drops they flow and water the earth. So too we have heard about locusts: when a diligent angel urged them on, after they had ravaged many towns, at the border of another place he delivered them to destruction. The scourge that had crushed many was itself crushed and cast down by another stronger than it. For a great wind stirred against it and first prevented it from entering the place; after that he struck it and covered it with a cloud of hailstones, and made it like heaps [?] of those slain by the sword. And the diligent angel saved the place with all its inhabitants. Let these things be as I have said. But what will you answer to that other objection: those who, because of negligence or the bad habits of places, those of many days

and nature has shown them to be [?] with respect to death. These, on the other hand, it has made short-lived [?] and weak in strength; and likewise other regions, because of their climate, raise people who are skilful and quick. So as not to make our discourse long, these things are passed down from hand to hand: for all those born in any region of this universe, whether their lives are shortened or lengthened, whether they are handsome or ugly, bold or modest, and for the way of life of each region or the customs of the peoples, what then? Has the law of providence perished, and is nature moved or set in motion by itself? Not at all. Nature runs according to the Word that sets it in being. As for human beings, their life is measured out to them according to what is beneficial from God; their conduct, however, they determine for themselves as they think and as they will. As for life, does the sun not measure it out to the Ethiopian as well? Let this teach you: among them too whole troops pass down to Sheol, and infants are snatched from life. And sometimes, through a great plague, many towns and many people pass away. Or are there places among them where no troop goes down to Sheol, and no youth, not even an infant, dies before his day? That supposition is altogether false. For in the same way as for everyone, the seasons that govern the world are fixed for them as well. Even in the north, lives are measured out to the inhabitants according to what helps them, and among them old men too are found vigorous by providence. Beauty and understanding, along with sharpness and strength, which are found from place to place, we attribute to climate. For freedom, if it comes from the mind, is not held back in those regions where the sun's furnace is fierce upon a person. But when it gathers itself there, it makes his color ugly, his body lean and parched, and from this he becomes rough and restless. For another man freedom turns the other way, and in temperate regions it assigns him his way of life; and having been raised in shade and cool air, he shows himself elegant and fair in complexion. Yet even when freedom acts in this way, if it is not helped by the height of providence, it turns from beauty to ugliness, through illness or through some

other cause. It is ruined [?] in strength, and providence confuses and maddens the mind, resists the climates of places and ways of life, lifts up through trials and adversities, and drives people out of their native constitution. And the great King delights in these things, as He judges the world as He wills, and leads it here and there for what is helpful, while in everything He trades for the advantage of our lives. He placed certain causes in nature, the begetter of all, so that with them and through them earthly lives come forth. He established the sun as the source of light, and He bound the soul in blood and limbs. Yet He did not do this because the variations of these things make the soul, so that we should say that they are the soul's creators. Likewise, even if climate is something allotted to nature, so that one thing comes about in this way and another in that, we do not strip the work of the world of the commands of governance. Rather, like what is owed to a law [?], it, together with its causes, must be bound by its Maker. So much for these things, and this is the argument. If it is sufficient, thanks be to the One who granted it. If not, let some other lover of labor take up other points and help our discourse. As for us, let us turn for the present to other questions and examine them as far as we are able.

It is well known that when we suffer losses, something [?] befalls us. Antony said: "Tell me, O Spirit who dwells in the high heavens, who holds the ends of the great world, who protects the saints, and who enables seeing eyes to find these things: what is the reason that, when two wicked men were walking along the road and a great storm came upon them, with sulphurous lightnings flashing, one of them went to destruction while the other found final salvation?" Through the mouth of a pious man the Spirit answered him this: the Lord knew beforehand and from the beginning that the one who perished would never repent, and would not profit from the blow that struck his companion, so He made him die. But of the one who was spared, He knew that the agitation of fear would draw him away from wickedness, bring him near to virtue, and show him the fruits of virtue. Antony asked again whether the one struck by lightning had any advantage from the virtue and profit of the one

who was spared. And again the Spirit enlightened him in mysteries by bringing another example: "If, of two sinners, one is swallowed up so that the other may be pricked [?], it is just before God that their advantage should be shared: that the blow of the one who was swallowed and the virtue of the one who feared should be placed in the middle in common and divided into portions." Again he pressed this question: why did one man, a greedy man, who had been swallowed up and had received myriads of swords and blows, escape death, while another, who only saw a battle, went down to Sheol from fear? And to this [?] from the mind he spoke, setting out what is beneficial and helpful. For to the first, the Father appointed swords and blows as a help. Or did not many rejoice to be joined to the craftsmen of holiness because of the sufferings of persecution? But to the second, the time of departure was a help. For He knew that his life would bring forth loss and damage if he went on living in the passing world. Hence one man, though sorely pressed by pains and calling Sheol his mother, He did not take out of life; while another He led away and removed even though life was still sweet to him; and Hezekiah is a great example of this. Again it was asked: why does He leave the evil and unjust man alone for a long time, and allow him to live a life of sin? And to this he answered: so that, like a bitter rod in their hands, many may be purified from wickedness. So it is with the lawyers of this world at times: having swallowed up weak men and stripped widows and orphans of houses and fields, another wicked man came upon them, bore down on them for a great deal of money, and brought them to [?]. Again I saw something, and I recount it for the benefit of many: a whole army, though magnificently armed, He let go into the hands of weak men and allowed a sentence full of justice, and they brought about its end and destruction. That army was entirely wicked. For when men from the land of the Assyrians, worthless in their crafts and defiled in their deeds, took up arms against the barbarians, they made a merciless resolve [?] that they would violate the barbarians' wives like beasts of the herd and would have no pity on them or on the children of their womb. Then the power of the Lord strengthened those barbarians, unsociable men and lovers of devastation, and they brought about the Assyrians' end. And for their long-standing evils these received a single requital: slaughter at the hands of barbarians. Again, concerning infants who die before their time, as we would put it,

Antony sought an explanation. And for this he found five reasons in all, according to the account of the Fathers. First: when God rebukes a wicked parent. For it says that He rebuked David and killed his son as the child of adultery, so that the fruit would not be a ruinous example to many. Second: if He sees that the cunning love of money is measured and abundant in the parents because of the children being born. For we see many who perish from worry and anxiety over money and give their children as the reason. Others acquire even when they have no children; and these are reproved by those, and those by these who have no children, and so the pretext for this greed [?] is exposed. Third: when He sees their wickedness and has pity on a righteous father, so that the fruit of sin may not grow. Fourth: if they were going to be more unjust than anyone else, and somehow perfect in wickedness. Fifth: so that the heavenly assembly may be completed [?] through those who are called; and for this reason He takes them, as sinless ones, to that wedding feast [?], so that it may lack nothing, and the hundred sheep may be of full number. These reasons the saints have stated. And whether by this one or that one, or perhaps by another, or by this or that, God removes the infant from the conduct of this life. But if anyone, regarding these words as insufficient, presses on toward the inscrutable judgments, let him keep a rein on his mind and listen also to the saying of the great Antony. For when he prayed earnestly that the Lord would show him what the departure from life that befalls infants means, this answer was given him: "Antony, know yourself; do not search into My judgments." Hence we too bind the explanation to its cause with a "perhaps," a "possibly," or a "it may be"; and so, not from ourselves, we [?] the explanation. Thus said Antony.

It has been allotted to me [?] for our benefit to take up also the question of wealth and poverty, and to say, as far as my feeble power allows, whether all wealth is from God. For I have heard many ask this, and it is asked of me and of others. Of wealth, one kind is acquired through providence and help from above, from God; another through permission and by free will.

Of free will, one kind comes through diligence and orderly labor, whether of trade or of crafts; another through fraud. Another kind of wealth comes from calumny; another from adversity and [?], when God permits it. He permits and lets it go when the one acquiring it is not skilled, or else He permits it so that freedom may be tested. For many people, when they are stung by bitterness and by times of need, gaze at the rich with a bitter eye full of envy and say: "If God had given me wealth, I would have managed it very generously and profitably." And so God permits this to happen to them, judging freedom and its words, so that it may not hold out [?] in its wickedness. And so that my discourse may not stray from its aim, I return and run through, by way of illustration, the headings of the division just stated. Wealth given by God is like that of the righteous. As that great one of the Hebrews said concerning Isaac: he sowed barley and brought in a hundredfold of barley, and the Lord blessed him, and the man grew great. And again concerning Job: the Lord added double to all that he had. And other such cases. Wealth from craft and handiwork is like that of those who cast statues, or are skilled in royal paintings, or similar things by which great men are valued. In this way they too acquire it: farmers, field-workers [?], carpenters, plasterers, sword-polishers and glassmakers; in short, every art and craft by which those who practise it are of good use, and by which they double their profit and increase their gain. Of the same sort are [?], or money-changers, and those who travel from place to place for foreign goods, whether by ship or by caravan [?], and the like. Wealth from trade is accompanied by diligence, care and measured toil, but not in the same way as for craftsmen; rather, shrewdness, contentiousness and much skill and learning are good for this above everything. And when freedom is diligent and industrious, it is not at all left without strength [?] by God, even though in this place and among men, as some philosopher said, there are those who toil, run and labor, and in everything fall behind and are left over.

Sin too accompanies trade, as another said: between buying and selling sins are wedged, as a peg enters between one stone and its neighbor. The merchant is not acquitted of sins; he constantly stands amid blemishes and lies, and constantly walks in hidden and unseen frauds. The fourth kind of wealth is that which is gathered by frauds and robberies, like that of governors and their lawyers, and that of robbers and bandits. It does not remain as in abundance, because it is mingled with the tears of strangers, and sometimes even with the blood of families. As the wise man again said: possessions gained by iniquity dwindle, but what is gathered in righteousness increases. And as the victorious Job said: "I have seen the wicked prospering, and suddenly his dwelling was plundered. His sons will be far from the commandments," and so on. The fifth kind of wealth is that which is gathered through demons, like that of enchanters and Chaldeans, diviners and sorcerers, those who foretell the future, examiners, astrologers and stargazers. For the wealth of these is gathered from the wages of sin, and from a demon who reveals the treasures of many. For example: someone is travelling, and his load is carried off by bandits. He comes to the sorcerer and promises him a thousand pieces of silver, or half of his load. Satan, the father of sin, who seized the bandit so that he would plot at the crossing and rob him, knows who robbed the merchant, whether in a house or on the road; and so he reveals it to the Chaldean, and when his work is praised, he is given what was asked. In the same way demons show their accomplished disciples treasures hidden in the earth. And if, after taking these, they want later to pray to the Lord and remove the former servitude from their neck, he takes the wealth away and carries it off from them, through the bearing of a burden, or bandits, or captors, or something else. And for this reason he does not give or reveal to many sorcerers the hidden treasures kept in the chambers of the earth, so that they may not be freed from need and turn aside from the yoke of the wicked one. Rather he keeps afflicting them constantly with worry and need, so that they may be enslaved to him and serve his wickedness. And hence there are also

needy Chaldeans. But why, when my aim is to examine the causes of wealth, have I been drawn down to poverty and need?
