The sixth kind of wealth is the one they call a matter of luck and fortune, when permission comes from Him who holds all things, as if to test freedom. For example, someone digging a cistern or cutting a well finds a treasure of gold or silver; or someone grazing donkeys or cows in ruined places, and the like, as they tell of a hunter; or someone who, buying fish from some boys, dragged up and drew out in their net a golden tripod [?]. Or as they tell of the king of the Samians: his ancestral signet ring fell into the [?] waters and the depths of the inner sea, and at once a fisherman, unknowingly, sold it in a fish to the king's house. These finds, and others like them, have given wealth and prosperity to many. And by permission, or by a diligent hand, everything is acquired. These are the kinds and general headings from which material wealth is gathered for the children of the earth, as if in abundance. In some cases, however, apart from these kinds mentioned, we find wealth acquired, as with a tutor or a priest, or a lyre-player [?], or a daughter of the craft of Aphrodite, or a powerful king, or a famous general who takes bribes from the powerful in the presence of the victors. Sometimes, too, many bring gifts of love to someone excellent in his craft and eminent in his line, and from this much wealth comes into his hand. We see a rich monk, just as we also see a greedy chief. For me, however, every kind of wealth is reckoned under the chain of greed, except the first motion, which is either given by God or acquired by toil. The rest are to me the bonds of the wicked one and equal to the fire of Sodom. And do not tell me that so-and-so is a chief priest and so-and-so a scribe. For if his heart and hand are distracted by money or by the purse, he is wretched in my eyes and a son of the left hand. These, then, are the kinds of wealth. Of poverty there are three sides. The first is a furnace of testing kindled by God upon a person, either

for testing, as with the good, or for the chastisement of iniquity, as with the wicked. For money is material for all despicable deeds, though not for everyone. And for this reason the Lord either prevents a person from acquiring it, or afterwards takes it from us. The second kind comes upon the wicked from slackness of hand and sluggishness. The third comes from free will, and it runs through many places. The first of these, and a good one, is the one who for the glory of heavenly wealth and the hope of rewards beyond chooses to become poor, like the need of Elijah and the poverty of the apostles. The second, and an evil one, is the one whose shameful desires make him poor, like the bands of debauchees and the swaggering lovers of luxury, who have squandered ancestral treasures and the stores of the diligent so as to fill the pleasure-loving belly with wine and to satisfy the lust of passion. What was stored up was used up, and what they longed for and loved they never reached. By the drinking of wine drunkenness only increases, and the fire of lust burns all the more with its fuel. The third kind of need, which is a middle sort, neither evil nor good, belongs to those who, for the empty praise of this world of vanity [?], become great-souled beyond what is measured, and spend everything they have before people's eyes so as to hunt praise from everyone. This kind, because it does not happen for the sake of the good, is not crowned as good; but because it brings profit and fruit to many, neither is it called evil, although we and all those in the Church call this kind evil. These are the kinds of poverty. If there is anything else by which a wretched man sees the misery of need, whether the harshness of [?], or a year of drought [?] that has ruined lands of their produce, or an illness that befalls a man alone, the one who was trained [?] and was plundered on its account, or someone swallowed up by the greed of thieves or bandits, all these and the like belong under those first two ways of need. Let us say, then, that it is for being tested or for being chastised that we distinguish and lay open these kinds,

so that no one, taking up their notions, should say that all wealth is from God, and make God a partner of bandits, Chaldeans and wicked men. For He has given us freedom of will, and has endowed it with power [?], and He lets it go until He judges it: when the mind is moved and does whatever the mind fills itself with and acts upon. He does not restrain the robber even when his wicked hand is raised against another's wealth, for He is testing all the more the one who is stripped of wealth, by need and misery. And if a man has made poverty the material for blasphemy, He takes it away and gives him abundance in its place. But if there is a grumbler who, as soon as he becomes rich, kills, commits adultery and does other wicked things, He heals him by binding him with the chain of poverty. Another man who used wealth well, was a just steward of mammon, and was merciful and compassionate in will and hand, He increases and blesses in all that he acquires, and extends his abundance from generation to generation, in jubilee. And if after his death his children waste it, and make their father's just inheritance the material for their sin, He takes it away, bows them down and humbles them under the heavy yoke of enduring poverty, which to every man alike is hateful and wearisome, fearsome before it is felt, something to flee from after it is felt, and precious in memory once we escape it. But because there are many who, having been shaken under the yoke of need and having experienced its bitter sufferings and how heavily it humiliates a person before the faces of many, remember its trial once they have become prosperous, to these the Lord distributes wealth, knowing as the Knower of all that the memory of misery will draw them to compassion for their fellow men. Other poor people He knows the memory of poverty would make close-fisted and hard toward the purse, and that the memory of the sufferings of need would stir up envy in them rather than mercy; and so the yoke is not lifted from them. In these adversities and others like them, I mean illness and health,

weakness and strength, deficiency and abundance of the senses, cunning and simplicity, beauty and ugliness, rule and subjection, or lordship and slavery, and any other opposites there may be, the all-knowing Helmsman judges, and guides and steers the nature of human beings here and there and in every way; in all things, toward salvation and what is most beneficial. Rather, let us give thanks. And with every limb let us offer the gift of thanksgiving and the pure sacrifice of praise, magnifying Him in wonder and amazement, and saying these things in astonishment:

O arm of the world and its foundation; O holder of the ends and governor of this universe; O guide and director of human intelligence and understanding, and maker of understandings; O mind wholly incomprehensible, Word that escapes word, and Spirit who established the immaterial spirits; O God of human beings, who are Yours, Lord and merciful Father; O immeasurable goodness and fountain of all love; who, keeping our affairs in justice and grace, give the grace that conquers, guide freedom on the path of providence, bring it out, as Your own image, from the snares of the slanderer, and alone, as a good physician, cleanse it from the defilement of shameful evils, and as watcher [?] and fountain of contemplation establish it free from the snares that lie in contemplation. O ruler of the great city, Father and Maker of the worlds to come, giver of wisdom and light to all beings, which, having come into being in You, also exist in You always, and whose spiritual nourishment is extended to them from You and by Your hands. O shoot equal to its Begetter, by whom good powers are made to sprout and through whom they spring up [?], as they draw knowledge from the fountain of the streams, and are enabled both to be made to sprout and to sprout, to drink from the light of knowledge and pass it on to another. O Trinity and Only One, who remain wholly Yourself, with all that is from You, beyond our lowliness, and from whom we receive only as much as we are able to grasp of Your acts toward us. At the same time, You have done and still do such wonders in us and toward us that we become worthy to attain You, if indeed we ourselves show from here on that we are worthy of this. And through love of labor
we cleanse our filthiness.
Here end the four discourses on idleness.
They were composed by Antony, the monk of Tagrit, whose fathers' family is descended from Gurgan.
